<div dir="auto">
<p>Khronos posts the AsciiDoc source of the glTF specification to enable
community feedback and remixing under CC-BY 4.0. Published versions of
the Specification are located in the <a
href="https://www.khronos.org/registry/glTF" rel="nofollow">glTF
Registry</a>.</p>

## 2. Introduction

<a href="#2-introduction" id="user-content-2-introduction"
class="anchor" aria-label="Permalink: 2. Introduction"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

### 2.1. General

<a href="#21-general" id="user-content-21-general" class="anchor"
aria-label="Permalink: 2.1. General"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

This document, referred to as the “glTF Specification” or just the
“Specification” hereafter, describes the glTF file format.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

glTF is an API-neutral runtime asset delivery format. glTF bridges the
gap between 3D content creation tools and modern graphics applications
by providing an efficient, extensible, interoperable format for the
transmission and loading of 3D content.

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

### 2.2. Document Conventions

<a href="#22-document-conventions"
id="user-content-22-document-conventions" class="anchor"
aria-label="Permalink: 2.2. Document Conventions"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

The glTF Specification is intended for use by both implementers of the
asset exporters or converters (e.g., digital content creation tools) and
application developers seeking to import or load glTF assets, forming a
basis for interoperability between these parties.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Specification text can address either party; typically, the intended
audience can be inferred from context, though some sections are defined
to address only one of these parties.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Any requirements, prohibitions, recommendations, or options defined by
[normative terminology](#introduction-normative-terminology) are imposed
only on the audience of that text.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

#### 2.2.1. Normative Terminology and References

<a href="#221-normative-terminology-and-references"
id="user-content-221-normative-terminology-and-references"
class="anchor"
aria-label="Permalink: 2.2.1. Normative Terminology and References"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

The key words **MUST**, **MUST NOT**, **REQUIRED**, **SHALL**, **SHALL
NOT**, **SHOULD**, **SHOULD NOT**, **RECOMMENDED**, **MAY**, and
**OPTIONAL** in this document are to be interpreted as described in [BCP
14](#bcp14).

</div>

<div dir="auto">

These key words are highlighted in the specification for clarity.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

References to external documents are considered normative if the
Specification uses any of the normative terms defined in this section to
refer to them or their requirements, either as a whole or in part.

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

#### 2.2.2. Informative Language

<a href="#222-informative-language"
id="user-content-222-informative-language" class="anchor"
aria-label="Permalink: 2.2.2. Informative Language"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Some language in the specification is purely informative, intended to
give background or suggestions to implementers or developers.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

If an entire chapter or section contains only informative language, its
title is suffixed with “(Informative)”. If not designated as
informative, all chapters, sections, and appendices in this document are
normative.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

All Notes, Implementation notes, and Examples are purely informative.

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

#### 2.2.3. Technical Terminology

<a href="#223-technical-terminology"
id="user-content-223-technical-terminology" class="anchor"
aria-label="Permalink: 2.2.3. Technical Terminology"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

The glTF Specification makes use of linear algebra terms such as
**axis**, **matrix**, **vector**, etc. to identify certain math
constructs and their behaviors as defined in the [International
Electrotechnical Vocabulary](#iev).

</div>

<div dir="auto">

The glTF Specification makes use of common engineering and graphics
terms such as **image**, **buffer**, **texture**, etc. to identify and
describe certain *glTF* constructs and their attributes, states, and
behaviors. This section defines the basic meanings of these terms in the
context of the Specification. The Specification text provides fuller
definitions of the terms and elaborates, extends, or clarifies the
definitions. When a term defined in this section is used in normative
language within the Specification, the definitions within the
Specification govern and supersede any meanings the terms may have in
other technical contexts (i.e. outside the Specification).

</div>

<div dir="auto">

accessor  
An object describing the number and the format of data elements stored
in a binary buffer.

animation  
An object describing the keyframe data, including timestamps, and the
target property affected by it.

back-facing  
See facingness.

buffer  
An external or embedded resource that represents a linear array of
bytes.

buffer view  
An object that represents a range of a specific buffer, and optional
metadata that controls how the buffer’s content is interpreted.

camera  
An object defining the projection parameters that are used to render a
scene.

facingness  
A classification of a triangle as either front-facing or back-facing,
depending on the orientation (winding order) of its vertices.

front-facing  
See facingness.

image  
A two dimensional array of pixels encoded as a standardized bitstream,
such as [PNG](#png).

indexed geometry  
A mesh primitive that uses a separate source of data (index values) to
assemble the primitive’s topology.

linear blend skinning  
A skinning method that computes a per-vertex transformation matrix as a
linear weighted sum of transformation matrices of the designated nodes.

material  
A parametrized approximation of visual properties of the real-world
object being represented by a mesh primitive.

mesh  
A collection of mesh primitives.

mesh primitive  
An object binding indexed or non-indexed geometry with a material.

mipmap  
A set of image representations consecutively reduced by the factor of 2
in each dimension.

morph target  
An altered state of a mesh primitive defined as a set of difference
values for its vertex attributes.

node  
An object defining the hierarchy relations and the local transform of
its content.

non-indexed geometry  
A mesh primitive that uses linear order of vertex attribute values to
assemble the primitive’s topology.

normal  
A unit XYZ vector defining the perpendicular to the surface.

root node  
A node that is not a child of any other node.

sampler  
An object that controls how image data is sampled.

scene  
An object containing a list of root nodes to render.

skinning  
The process of computing and applying individual transforms for each
vertex of a mesh primitive.

tangent  
A unit XYZ vector defining a tangential direction on the surface.

texture  
An object that combines an image and its sampler.

topology type  
State that controls how vertices are assembled, e.g. as lists of
triangles, strips of lines, etc.

vertex attribute  
A property associated with a vertex.

winding order  
The relative order in which vertices are defined within a triangle

wrapping  
A process of selecting an image pixel based on normalized texture
coordinates.

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

### 2.3. Motivation and Design Goals (Informative)

<a href="#23-motivation-and-design-goals-informative"
id="user-content-23-motivation-and-design-goals-informative"
class="anchor"
aria-label="Permalink: 2.3. Motivation and Design Goals (Informative)"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

glTF is an open interoperable 3D asset ‘transmission’ format that is
compact, and efficient to process and render at runtime. glTF 2.0 is
designed to be vendor- and runtime-neutral, usable by a wide variety of
native and web-based engines and applications regardless of underlying
platforms and 3D graphics APIs.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

glTF’s focus on run-time efficiency is a different design goal than
typical 3D ‘authoring’ formats. Authoring formats are typically more
verbose, with higher processing overheads, to carry authoring data that
is no longer needed after iterative design is complete. glTF is
complementary to authoring formats, providing a common, interoperable
distillation target for publishing 3D assets to a wide audience of end
users.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

A primary goal of glTF is to be deployable on a wide range of devices
and platforms, including the web and mobile devices with limited
processing and memory resources. glTF can be evolved, to keep pace with
growing compute capabilities over time. This helps to foster broad
industry consensus on 3D functionality that can be used ubiquitously,
including Physically Based Rendering.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

glTF combines an easily parsable JSON scene description with one or more
binary resources representing geometry, animations, and other rich data.
These binary resources can often be loaded directly into GPU buffers
with no additional parsing or processing, combining the faithful
preservation of full hierarchical scenes, nodes, meshes, cameras,
materials, and animations with efficient delivery and fast loading.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

glTF has been designed to meet the following goals:

</div>

<div dir="auto">

- **Compact file sizes.** The plain text glTF JSON file description is
  compact and rapid to parse. All large data such as geometry, textures
  and animations are stored in binary files that are significantly
  smaller than equivalent text representations.

- **Runtime-independence.** glTF is purely an asset format and does not
  mandate any runtime behavior. This enables its use by any application
  for any purpose, including display using any rendering technology, up
  to and including path tracing renderers.

- **Complete 3D scene representation.** Not restricted to single
  objects, glTF can represent entire scenes, including nodes,
  transformations, transform hierarchy, meshes, materials, cameras, and
  animations.

- **Extensibility.** glTF is fully extensible, enabling the addition of
  both general-purpose and vendor-specific extensions, including
  geometry and texture compression. Widely adopted extensions may be
  considered for integration into future versions of the glTF
  specification.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

The following are outside the scope of glTF 2.0:

</div>

<div dir="auto">

- **glTF is not a streaming format.** The binary data in glTF is
  inherently streamable, and the buffer design allows for fetching data
  incrementally, but there are no other streaming constructs in glTF
  2.0.

- **glTF is not an authoring format.** glTF deliberately does not retain
  3D authoring information, in order to preserve runtime efficiency,
  however glTF files may be ingested by 3D authoring tools for remixing.

- **glTF is not intended to be human-readable,** though by virtue of
  being represented in JSON, it is developer-friendly.

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

### 2.4. glTF Basics

<a href="#24-gltf-basics" id="user-content-24-gltf-basics"
class="anchor" aria-label="Permalink: 2.4. glTF Basics"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

A glTF asset is represented by:

</div>

<div dir="auto">

- A JSON-formatted file (`.gltf`) containing a full scene description:
  node hierarchy, materials, cameras, as well as descriptor information
  for meshes, animations, and other constructs.

- Binary files (`.bin`) containing geometry, animation, and other
  buffer-based data.

- Image files (`.jpg`, `.png`) containing texture images.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Binary and image resources **MAY** also be embedded directly in JSON
using [Data URI](#data-uri) or stored side-by-side with JSON in
[GLB](#glb-file-format-specification) container.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

A valid glTF asset **MUST** specify its version.

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

### 2.5. Versioning

<a href="#25-versioning" id="user-content-25-versioning" class="anchor"
aria-label="Permalink: 2.5. Versioning"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Any updates made to the glTF Specification in a minor version **MUST**
be backward and forward compatible. Backward compatibility means that
any client implementation that supports loading a glTF 2.x asset will
also be able to load a glTF 2.0 asset. Forward compatibility means that
a client implementation that only supports glTF 2.0 can load glTF 2.x
assets while gracefully ignoring any new features it does not
understand.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

A minor version update **MAY** introduce new features but **MUST NOT**
change any previously existing behavior. Existing functionality **MAY**
be deprecated in a minor version update, but it **MUST NOT** be removed.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Major version updates **MAY** be incompatible with previous versions.

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

### 2.6. File Extensions and Media Types

<a href="#26-file-extensions-and-media-types"
id="user-content-26-file-extensions-and-media-types" class="anchor"
aria-label="Permalink: 2.6. File Extensions and Media Types"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

- [JSON](#json) glTF files **SHOULD** use `.gltf` extension and
  [`model/gltf+json`](#gltf-json) Media Type.

- glTF files stored in [GLB](#glb-file-format-specification) container
  **SHOULD** use `.glb` extension and
  [`model/gltf-binary`](#gltf-binary) Media Type.

- Files representing binary buffers **SHOULD** use either:

  <div dir="auto">

  - `.bin` file extension with
    [`application/octet-stream`](#octet-stream) Media Type;

  - `.bin`, `.glbin`, or `.glbuf` file extensions with
    [`application/gltf-buffer`](#gltf-buffer) Media Type.

  </div>

- [PNG](#png) images **SHOULD** use `.png` file extension with
  [`image/png`](#image-png) Media Type;

  <div dir="auto">

  - PNG images **SHOULD NOT** contain animations, non-square pixel
    ratios, or embedded ICC profiles. Such features, if present,
    **MUST** be ignored by client implementations.

  </div>

- [JPEG](#jpeg) images **SHOULD** use `.jpeg` or `.jpg` file extensions
  with [`image/jpeg`](#image-jpeg) Media Type

  <div dir="auto">

  - JPEG images **MUST** be compatible with [JPEG File Interchange
    Format](#jfif).

  - JPEG images **SHOULD NOT** contain embedded ICC profiles. If
    present, embedded ICC profiles **MUST** be ignored by client
    implementations.

  - [Exchangeable image file format (Exif)](#exif) chunks **MAY** be
    ignored by client implementations.

    <div dir="auto">

    <table>
    <colgroup>
    <col style="width: 50%" />
    <col style="width: 50%" />
    </colgroup>
    <tbody>
    <tr>
    <td><div dir="auto">
    Note
    </div></td>
    <td><div dir="auto">
    Implementation Note
    </div>
    <div dir="auto">
    <p>Certain Exif chunks, e.g., “Orientation”, may severely impact an
    asset’s portability.</p>
    </div></td>
    </tr>
    </tbody>
    </table>

    </div>

  </div>

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

### 2.7. JSON Encoding

<a href="#27-json-encoding" id="user-content-27-json-encoding"
class="anchor" aria-label="Permalink: 2.7. JSON Encoding"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Although glTF Specification does not define any subset of the
[JSON](#json) format, implementations **SHOULD** be aware of its
peculiar properties that could affect asset interoperability.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

1.  glTF JSON data **SHOULD** be written with UTF-8 encoding without
    BOM. This requirement is not applied when a glTF implementation does
    not control string encoding. glTF implementations **SHOULD** adhere
    to [RFC 8259](#json), Section 8.1. with regards to treating BOM
    presence.

2.  ASCII characters stored in glTF JSON **SHOULD** be written without
    JSON escaping.

    <div dir="auto">

    <table>
    <colgroup>
    <col style="width: 50%" />
    <col style="width: 50%" />
    </colgroup>
    <tbody>
    <tr>
    <td><div dir="auto">
    Note
    </div></td>
    <td><div dir="auto">
    Example
    </div>
    <div dir="auto">
    <p><code>"buffer"</code> instead of
    <code>"\u0062\u0075\u0066\u0066\u0065\u0072"</code>.</p>
    </div></td>
    </tr>
    </tbody>
    </table>

    </div>

3.  Non-ASCII characters stored in glTF JSON **MAY** be escaped.

    <div dir="auto">

    <table>
    <colgroup>
    <col style="width: 50%" />
    <col style="width: 50%" />
    </colgroup>
    <tbody>
    <tr>
    <td><div dir="auto">
    Note
    </div></td>
    <td><div dir="auto">
    Example
    </div>
    <div dir="auto">
    <p>These two examples represent the same glTF JSON data.</p>
    </div>
    <div dir="auto">
    <div dir="auto">
    <div
    class="highlight highlight-source-json notranslate position-relative overflow-auto"
    dir="auto" data-snippet-clipboard-copy-content="{
        &quot;asset&quot;: {
            &quot;version&quot;: &quot;2.0&quot;
        },
        &quot;nodes&quot;: [
            {
                &quot;name&quot;: &quot;куб&quot;
            },
            {
                &quot;name&quot;: &quot;立方體&quot;
            }
        ]
    }">
    <pre><code>{
        &quot;asset&quot;: {
            &quot;version&quot;: &quot;2.0&quot;
        },
        &quot;nodes&quot;: [
            {
                &quot;name&quot;: &quot;куб&quot;
            },
            {
                &quot;name&quot;: &quot;立方體&quot;
            }
        ]
    }</code></pre>
    </div>
    </div>
    </div>
    <div dir="auto">
    <div dir="auto">
    <div
    class="highlight highlight-source-json notranslate position-relative overflow-auto"
    dir="auto" data-snippet-clipboard-copy-content="{
        &quot;asset&quot;: {
            &quot;version&quot;: &quot;2.0&quot;
        },
        &quot;nodes&quot;: [
            {
                &quot;name&quot;: &quot;\u043a\u0443\u0431&quot;
            },
            {
                &quot;name&quot;: &quot;\u7acb\u65b9\u9ad4&quot;
            }
        ]
    }">
    <pre><code>{
        &quot;asset&quot;: {
            &quot;version&quot;: &quot;2.0&quot;
        },
        &quot;nodes&quot;: [
            {
                &quot;name&quot;: &quot;\u043a\u0443\u0431&quot;
            },
            {
                &quot;name&quot;: &quot;\u7acb\u65b9\u9ad4&quot;
            }
        ]
    }</code></pre>
    </div>
    </div>
    </div></td>
    </tr>
    </tbody>
    </table>

    </div>

4.  Property names (keys) within JSON objects **SHOULD** be unique. glTF
    client implementations **SHOULD** override lexically preceding
    values for the same key.

5.  Some of glTF properties are defined as integers in the schema. Such
    values **MAY** be stored as decimals with a zero fractional part or
    by using exponent notation. Regardless of encoding, such properties
    **MUST NOT** contain any non-zero fractional value.

    <div dir="auto">

    <table>
    <colgroup>
    <col style="width: 50%" />
    <col style="width: 50%" />
    </colgroup>
    <tbody>
    <tr>
    <td><div dir="auto">
    Note
    </div></td>
    <td><div dir="auto">
    Example
    </div>
    <div dir="auto">
    <p><code>100</code>, <code>100.0</code>, and <code>1e2</code> represent
    the same value. See <a href="#json">RFC 8259</a>, Section 6 for more
    details.</p>
    </div></td>
    </tr>
    </tbody>
    </table>

    </div>

6.  Non-integer numbers **SHOULD** be written in a way that preserves
    original values when these numbers are read back, i.e., they
    **SHOULD NOT** be altered by JSON serialization / deserialization
    roundtrip.

    <div dir="auto">

    <table>
    <colgroup>
    <col style="width: 50%" />
    <col style="width: 50%" />
    </colgroup>
    <tbody>
    <tr>
    <td><div dir="auto">
    Note
    </div></td>
    <td><div dir="auto">
    Implementation Note
    </div>
    <div dir="auto">
    <p>This is typically achieved with algorithms like Grisu2 used by common
    JSON libraries.</p>
    </div></td>
    </tr>
    </tbody>
    </table>

    </div>

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

### 2.8. URIs

<a href="#28-uris" id="user-content-28-uris" class="anchor"
aria-label="Permalink: 2.8. URIs"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

glTF assets use [URIs](#uri) or [IRIs](#iri) to reference buffers and
image resources. Assets **MAY** contain at least these two URI types:

</div>

<div dir="auto">

- **Data URIs** that embed binary resources in the glTF JSON as defined
  by the [RFC 2397](#data-uri). The Data URI’s `mediatype` field
  **MUST** match the encoded content.

  <div dir="auto">

  <table>
  <colgroup>
  <col style="width: 50%" />
  <col style="width: 50%" />
  </colgroup>
  <tbody>
  <tr>
  <td><div dir="auto">
  Note
  </div></td>
  <td><div dir="auto">
  Implementation Note
  </div>
  <div dir="auto">
  <p>Base64 encoding used in Data URI increases the payload’s byte length
  by 33%.</p>
  </div></td>
  </tr>
  </tbody>
  </table>

  </div>

- **Relative paths** — `path-noscheme` or `ipath-noscheme` as defined by
  [RFC 3986](#uri), Section 4.2 or [RFC 3987](#iri), Section
  2.2 — without scheme, authority, or parameters. Reserved characters
  (as defined by [RFC 3986](#uri), Section 2.2. and [RFC 3987](#iri),
  Section 2.2.) **MUST** be percent-encoded.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Paths with non-ASCII characters **MAY** be written as-is, with JSON
string escaping, or with percent-encoding; all these options are valid.
For example, the following three paths point to the same resource:

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div dir="auto">

<div class="highlight highlight-source-json notranslate position-relative overflow-auto"
dir="auto" snippet-clipboard-copy-content="{
    &quot;images&quot;: [
        {
            &quot;uri&quot;: &quot;grande_sphère.png&quot;
        },
        {
            &quot;uri&quot;: &quot;grande_sph\u00E8re.png&quot;
        },
        {
            &quot;uri&quot;: &quot;grande_sph%C3%A8re.png&quot;
        }
    ]
}">

    {
        "images": [
            {
                "uri": "grande_sphère.png"
            },
            {
                "uri": "grande_sph\u00E8re.png"
            },
            {
                "uri": "grande_sph%C3%A8re.png"
            }
        ]
    }

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Client implementations **MAY** optionally support additional URI
components. For example `http://` or `file://` schemes, authorities,
hostnames, absolute paths, and query or fragment parameters. Assets
containing these additional URI components would be less portable.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 50%" />
<col style="width: 50%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><div dir="auto">
Note
</div></td>
<td><div dir="auto">
Implementation Note
</div>
<div dir="auto">
<p>This allows the application to decide the best approach for delivery:
if different assets share many of the same geometries, animations, or
textures, separate files may be preferred to reduce the total amount of
data requested. With separate files, applications may progressively load
data and do not need to load data for parts of a model that are not
visible. If an application cares more about single-file deployment,
embedding data may be preferred even though it increases the overall
size due to base64 encoding and does not support progressive or
on-demand loading. Alternatively, an asset could use the GLB container
to store JSON and binary data in one file without base64 encoding. See
<a href="#glb-file-format-specification">GLB File Format
Specification</a> for details.</p>
</div></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

URIs **SHOULD** undergo syntax-based normalization as defined by [RFC
3986](#uri), Section 6.2.2, [RFC 3987](#iri), Section 5.3.2, and
applicable schema rules (e.g., [RFC 7230](#http), Section 2.7.3 for
HTTP) on export and/or import.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 50%" />
<col style="width: 50%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><div dir="auto">
Note
</div></td>
<td><div dir="auto">
Implementation Note
</div>
<div dir="auto">
<p>While the specification does not explicitly disallow non-normalized
URIs, their use may be unsupported or lead to unwanted
side-effects — such as security warnings or cache misses — on some
platforms.</p>
</div></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

</div>

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

## 3. Concepts

<a href="#3-concepts" id="user-content-3-concepts" class="anchor"
aria-label="Permalink: 3. Concepts"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

### 3.1. General

<a href="#31-general" id="user-content-31-general" class="anchor"
aria-label="Permalink: 3.1. General"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

The figure below shows relations between top-level arrays in a glTF
asset. See the [Properties Reference](#properties-reference).

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div dir="auto">

<a
href="/KhronosGroup/glTF/blob/main/specification/2.0/figures/objects.svg"
target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer"><img
src="/KhronosGroup/glTF/raw/main/specification/2.0/figures/objects.svg"
style="max-width: 100%;" alt="objects" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Figure 1. glTF Object Hierarchy

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

### 3.2. Asset

<a href="#32-asset" id="user-content-32-asset" class="anchor"
aria-label="Permalink: 3.2. Asset"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Each glTF asset **MUST** have an `asset` property. The `asset` object
**MUST** contain a `version` property that specifies the target glTF
version of the asset. Additionally, an optional `minVersion` property
**MAY** be used to specify the minimum glTF version support required to
load the asset. The `minVersion` property allows asset creators to
specify a minimum version that a client implementation **MUST** support
in order to load the asset. This is very similar to the
`extensionsRequired` concept described in [Section
3.12](#specifying-extensions), where an asset **SHOULD NOT** be loaded
if the client does not support the specified extension. Additional
metadata **MAY** be stored in optional properties such as `generator` or
`copyright`. For example,

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div dir="auto">

<div class="highlight highlight-source-json notranslate position-relative overflow-auto"
dir="auto" snippet-clipboard-copy-content="{
    &quot;asset&quot;: {
        &quot;version&quot;: &quot;2.0&quot;,
        &quot;generator&quot;: &quot;collada2gltf@f356b99aef8868f74877c7ca545f2cd206b9d3b7&quot;,
        &quot;copyright&quot;: &quot;2017 (c) Khronos Group&quot;
    }
}">

    {
        "asset": {
            "version": "2.0",
            "generator": "collada2gltf@f356b99aef8868f74877c7ca545f2cd206b9d3b7",
            "copyright": "2017 (c) Khronos Group"
        }
    }

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 50%" />
<col style="width: 50%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><div dir="auto">
Note
</div></td>
<td><div dir="auto">
Implementation Note
</div>
<div dir="auto">
<p>Client implementations should first check whether a
<code>minVersion</code> property is specified and ensure both major and
minor versions can be supported. If no <code>minVersion</code> is
specified, then clients should check the <code>version</code> property
and ensure the major version is supported. Clients that load <a
href="#glb-file-format-specification">GLB format</a> should also check
for the <code>minVersion</code> and <code>version</code> properties in
the JSON chunk as the version specified in the GLB header only refers to
the GLB container version.</p>
</div></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

### 3.3. Indices and Names

<a href="#33-indices-and-names" id="user-content-33-indices-and-names"
class="anchor" aria-label="Permalink: 3.3. Indices and Names"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Entities of a glTF asset are referenced by their indices in
corresponding arrays, e.g., a `bufferView` refers to a `buffer` by
specifying the buffer’s index in `buffers` array. For example:

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div dir="auto">

<div class="highlight highlight-source-json notranslate position-relative overflow-auto"
dir="auto" snippet-clipboard-copy-content="{
    &quot;buffers&quot;: [
        {
            &quot;byteLength&quot;: 1024,
            &quot;uri&quot;: &quot;path-to.bin&quot;
        }
    ],
    &quot;bufferViews&quot;: [
        {
            &quot;buffer&quot;: 0,
            &quot;byteLength&quot;: 512,
            &quot;byteOffset&quot;: 0
        }
    ]
}">

    {
        "buffers": [
            {
                "byteLength": 1024,
                "uri": "path-to.bin"
            }
        ],
        "bufferViews": [
            {
                "buffer": 0,
                "byteLength": 512,
                "byteOffset": 0
            }
        ]
    }

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

In this example, `buffers` and `bufferViews` arrays have only one
element each. The bufferView refers to the buffer using the buffer’s
index: `"buffer": 0`.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Indices **MUST** be non-negative integer numbers. Indices **MUST**
always point to existing elements.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Whereas indices are used for internal glTF references, optional *names*
are used for application-specific uses such as display. Any top-level
glTF object **MAY** have a `name` string property for this purpose.
These property values are not guaranteed to be unique as they are
intended to contain values created when the asset was authored.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

For property names, glTF usually uses camel case, `likeThis`.

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

### 3.4. Coordinate System and Units

<a href="#34-coordinate-system-and-units"
id="user-content-34-coordinate-system-and-units" class="anchor"
aria-label="Permalink: 3.4. Coordinate System and Units"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

glTF uses a right-handed coordinate system. glTF defines +Y as up, +Z as
forward, and -X as right; the front of a glTF asset faces +Z.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div dir="auto">

<a
href="/KhronosGroup/glTF/blob/main/specification/2.0/figures/coordinate-system.png"
target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer"><img
src="/KhronosGroup/glTF/raw/main/specification/2.0/figures/coordinate-system.png"
style="max-width: 100%;" alt="coordinate system" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Figure 2. glTF Coordinate System Orientation

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

The units for all linear distances are meters.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

All angles are in radians.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Positive rotation is counterclockwise.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Red, Green, and Blue primary colors use [Recommendation ITU-R
BT.709](#bt709) chromaticity coordinates.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 50%" />
<col style="width: 50%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><div dir="auto">
Note
</div></td>
<td><div dir="auto">
Implementation Note
</div>
<div dir="auto">
<p>Chromaticity coordinates define the interpretation of each primary
color channel of the color model. In the context of a typical display,
color primaries describe the color of the red, green, and blue phosphors
or filters. Unless a wide color gamut output is explicitly used, client
implementations usually do not need to convert colors. Future
specification versions or extensions may allow other color primaries
(such as P3).</p>
</div></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

### 3.5. Scenes

<a href="#35-scenes" id="user-content-35-scenes" class="anchor"
aria-label="Permalink: 3.5. Scenes"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

#### 3.5.1. Overview

<a href="#351-overview" id="user-content-351-overview" class="anchor"
aria-label="Permalink: 3.5.1. Overview"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

glTF 2.0 assets **MAY** contain zero or more *scenes*, the set of visual
objects to render. Scenes are defined in a `scenes` array. All nodes
listed in `scene.nodes` array **MUST** be root nodes, i.e., they **MUST
NOT** be listed in a `node.children` array of any node. The same root
node **MAY** appear in multiple scenes.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

An additional root-level property, `scene` (note singular), identifies
which of the scenes in the array **SHOULD** be displayed at load time.
When `scene` is undefined, client implementations **MAY** delay
rendering until a particular scene is requested.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

A glTF asset that does not contain any scenes **SHOULD** be treated as a
library of individual entities such as materials or meshes.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

The following example defines a glTF asset with a single scene that
contains a single node.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div dir="auto">

<div class="highlight highlight-source-json notranslate position-relative overflow-auto"
dir="auto" snippet-clipboard-copy-content="{
    &quot;nodes&quot;: [
        {
            &quot;name&quot;: &quot;singleNode&quot;
        }
    ],
    &quot;scenes&quot;: [
        {
            &quot;name&quot;: &quot;singleScene&quot;,
            &quot;nodes&quot;: [
                0
            ]
        }
    ],
    &quot;scene&quot;: 0
}">

    {
        "nodes": [
            {
                "name": "singleNode"
            }
        ],
        "scenes": [
            {
                "name": "singleScene",
                "nodes": [
                    0
                ]
            }
        ],
        "scene": 0
    }

</div>

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

#### 3.5.2. Nodes and Hierarchy

<a href="#352-nodes-and-hierarchy"
id="user-content-352-nodes-and-hierarchy" class="anchor"
aria-label="Permalink: 3.5.2. Nodes and Hierarchy"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

glTF assets **MAY** define *nodes*, that is, the objects comprising the
scene to render.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Nodes **MAY** have transform properties, as described later.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Nodes are organized in a parent-child hierarchy known informally as the
*node hierarchy*. A node is called a *root node* when it doesn’t have a
parent.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

The node hierarchy **MUST** be a set of disjoint strict trees. That is
node hierarchy **MUST NOT** contain cycles and each node **MUST** have
zero or one parent node.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

The node hierarchy is defined using a node’s `children` property, as in
the following example:

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div dir="auto">

<div class="highlight highlight-source-json notranslate position-relative overflow-auto"
dir="auto" snippet-clipboard-copy-content="{
    &quot;nodes&quot;: [
        {
            &quot;name&quot;: &quot;Car&quot;,
            &quot;children&quot;: [1, 2, 3, 4]
        },
        {
            &quot;name&quot;: &quot;wheel_1&quot;
        },
        {
            &quot;name&quot;: &quot;wheel_2&quot;
        },
        {
            &quot;name&quot;: &quot;wheel_3&quot;
        },
        {
            &quot;name&quot;: &quot;wheel_4&quot;
        }
    ]
}">

    {
        "nodes": [
            {
                "name": "Car",
                "children": [1, 2, 3, 4]
            },
            {
                "name": "wheel_1"
            },
            {
                "name": "wheel_2"
            },
            {
                "name": "wheel_3"
            },
            {
                "name": "wheel_4"
            }
        ]
    }

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

The node named `Car` has four children. Each of those nodes could in
turn have its own children, creating a hierarchy of nodes.

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

#### 3.5.3. Transformations

<a href="#353-transformations" id="user-content-353-transformations"
class="anchor" aria-label="Permalink: 3.5.3. Transformations"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Any node **MAY** define a local space transform either by supplying a
`matrix` property, or any of `translation`, `rotation`, and `scale`
properties (also known as *TRS properties*). `translation` and `scale`
are 3D vectors in the local coordinate system. `rotation` is a unit
quaternion value, XYZW, in the local coordinate system, where W is the
scalar.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

When `matrix` is defined, it **MUST** be decomposable to TRS properties.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 50%" />
<col style="width: 50%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><div dir="auto">
Note
</div></td>
<td><div dir="auto">
Implementation Note
</div>
<div dir="auto">
<p>Transformation matrices cannot skew or shear.</p>
</div></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

When a node is targeted for animation (referenced by an
`animation.channel.target`), only TRS properties **MAY** be present;
`matrix` **MUST NOT** be present.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

To compose the local transformation matrix, TRS properties **MUST** be
converted to matrices and postmultiplied in the `T * R * S` order; first
the scale is applied to the vertices, then the rotation, and then the
translation.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 50%" />
<col style="width: 50%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><div dir="auto">
Note
</div></td>
<td><div dir="auto">
Implementation Note
</div>
<div dir="auto">
<p>Non-invertible transforms (e.g., scaling one axis to zero) could lead
to lighting and/or visibility artifacts.</p>
</div></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 50%" />
<col style="width: 50%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><div dir="auto">
Note
</div></td>
<td><div dir="auto">
Implementation Note
</div>
<div dir="auto">
<p>When the scale is zero on all three axes (by node transform or by
animated scale), implementations are free to optimize away rendering of
the node’s mesh, and all of the node’s children’s meshes. This provides
a mechanism to animate visibility. Skinned meshes must not use this
optimization unless all of the joints in the skin are scaled to zero
simultaneously.</p>
</div></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

The global transformation matrix of a node is the product of the global
transformation matrix of its parent node and its own local
transformation matrix. When the node has no parent node, its global
transformation matrix is identical to its local transformation matrix.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

In the example below, a node named `Box` defines non-default rotation
and translation.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div dir="auto">

<div class="highlight highlight-source-json notranslate position-relative overflow-auto"
dir="auto" snippet-clipboard-copy-content="{
    &quot;nodes&quot;: [
        {
            &quot;name&quot;: &quot;Box&quot;,
            &quot;rotation&quot;: [
                0,
                0,
                0,
                1
            ],
            &quot;scale&quot;: [
                1,
                1,
                1
            ],
            &quot;translation&quot;: [
                -17.7082,
                -11.4156,
                2.0922
            ]
        }
    ]
}">

    {
        "nodes": [
            {
                "name": "Box",
                "rotation": [
                    0,
                    0,
                    0,
                    1
                ],
                "scale": [
                    1,
                    1,
                    1
                ],
                "translation": [
                    -17.7082,
                    -11.4156,
                    2.0922
                ]
            }
        ]
    }

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

The next example defines the transform for a node with attached camera
using the `matrix` property rather than using the individual TRS values:

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div dir="auto">

<div class="highlight highlight-source-json notranslate position-relative overflow-auto"
dir="auto" snippet-clipboard-copy-content="{
    &quot;nodes&quot;: [
        {
            &quot;name&quot;: &quot;node-camera&quot;,
            &quot;camera&quot;: 1,
            &quot;matrix&quot;: [
                -0.99975,
                -0.00679829,
                0.0213218,
                0,
                0.00167596,
                0.927325,
                0.374254,
                0,
                -0.0223165,
                0.374196,
                -0.927081,
                0,
                -0.0115543,
                0.194711,
                -0.478297,
                1
            ]
        }
    ]
}">

    {
        "nodes": [
            {
                "name": "node-camera",
                "camera": 1,
                "matrix": [
                    -0.99975,
                    -0.00679829,
                    0.0213218,
                    0,
                    0.00167596,
                    0.927325,
                    0.374254,
                    0,
                    -0.0223165,
                    0.374196,
                    -0.927081,
                    0,
                    -0.0115543,
                    0.194711,
                    -0.478297,
                    1
                ]
            }
        ]
    }

</div>

</div>

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

### 3.6. Binary Data Storage

<a href="#36-binary-data-storage"
id="user-content-36-binary-data-storage" class="anchor"
aria-label="Permalink: 3.6. Binary Data Storage"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

#### 3.6.1. Buffers and Buffer Views

<a href="#361-buffers-and-buffer-views"
id="user-content-361-buffers-and-buffer-views" class="anchor"
aria-label="Permalink: 3.6.1. Buffers and Buffer Views"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

##### 3.6.1.1. Overview

<a href="#3611-overview" id="user-content-3611-overview" class="anchor"
aria-label="Permalink: 3.6.1.1. Overview"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

A **buffer** is arbitrary data stored as a binary blob. The buffer
**MAY** contain any combination of geometry, animation, skins, and
images.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Binary blobs allow efficient creation of GPU buffers and textures since
they require no additional parsing, except perhaps decompression.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

glTF assets **MAY** have any number of buffer resources. Buffers are
defined in the asset’s `buffers` array.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

While there’s no hard upper limit on buffer’s size, glTF assets **SHOULD
NOT** use buffers bigger than 2<sup>53</sup> bytes because some JSON
parsers may be unable to parse their `byteLength` correctly. Buffers
stored as [GLB](#glb-file-format-specification) binary chunk have an
implicit limit of 2<sup>32</sup>-1 bytes.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

All buffer data defined in this specification (i.e., geometry
attributes, geometry indices, sparse accessor data, animation inputs and
outputs, inverse bind matrices) **MUST** use little endian byte order.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

The following example defines a buffer. The `byteLength` property
specifies the size of the buffer file. The `uri` property is the URI to
the buffer data.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div dir="auto">

<div class="highlight highlight-source-json notranslate position-relative overflow-auto"
dir="auto" snippet-clipboard-copy-content="{
   &quot;buffers&quot;: [
       {
           &quot;byteLength&quot;: 102040,
           &quot;uri&quot;: &quot;duck.bin&quot;
       }
   ]
}">

    {
       "buffers": [
           {
               "byteLength": 102040,
               "uri": "duck.bin"
           }
       ]
    }

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

The byte length of the referenced resource **MUST** be greater than or
equal to the `buffer.byteLength` property.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Buffer data **MAY** alternatively be embedded in the glTF file via
`data:` URI with base64 encoding. When `data:` URI is used for buffer
storage, its `mediatype` field **MUST** be set to
`application/octet-stream` or `application/gltf-buffer`.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

A *buffer view* represents a contiguous segment of data in a buffer,
defined by a byte offset into the buffer specified in the `byteOffset`
property and a total byte length specified by the `byteLength` property
of the buffer view.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Buffer views used for images, vertex indices, vertex attributes, or
inverse bind matrices **MUST** contain only one kind of data, i.e., the
same buffer view **MUST NOT** be used both for vertex indices and vertex
attributes.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

When a buffer view is used by vertex indices or attribute accessors it
**SHOULD** specify `bufferView.target` with a value of *element array
buffer* or *array buffer* respectively.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 50%" />
<col style="width: 50%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><div dir="auto">
Note
</div></td>
<td><div dir="auto">
Implementation Note
</div>
<div dir="auto">
<p>This allows client implementations to early designate each buffer
view to a proper processing step, e.g, buffer views with vertex indices
and attributes would be copied to the appropriate GPU buffers, while
buffer views with image data would be passed to format-specific image
decoders.</p>
</div></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

The `bufferView.target` value uses integer enums defined in the
[Properties Reference](#_bufferview_target).

</div>

<div dir="auto">

The following example defines two buffer views: the first holds the
indices for an indexed triangle set, and the second holds the vertex
data for the triangle set.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div dir="auto">

<div class="highlight highlight-source-json notranslate position-relative overflow-auto"
dir="auto" snippet-clipboard-copy-content="{
    &quot;bufferViews&quot;: [
        {
            &quot;buffer&quot;: 0,
            &quot;byteLength&quot;: 25272,
            &quot;byteOffset&quot;: 0,
            &quot;target&quot;: 34963
        },
        {
            &quot;buffer&quot;: 0,
            &quot;byteLength&quot;: 76768,
            &quot;byteOffset&quot;: 25272,
            &quot;byteStride&quot;: 32,
            &quot;target&quot;: 34962
        }
    ]
}">

    {
        "bufferViews": [
            {
                "buffer": 0,
                "byteLength": 25272,
                "byteOffset": 0,
                "target": 34963
            },
            {
                "buffer": 0,
                "byteLength": 76768,
                "byteOffset": 25272,
                "byteStride": 32,
                "target": 34962
            }
        ]
    }

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

When a buffer view is used for vertex attribute data, it **MAY** have a
`byteStride` property. This property defines the stride in bytes between
each vertex. Buffer views with other types of data **MUST NOT** not
define `byteStride` (unless such layout is explicitly enabled by an
extension).

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Buffers and buffer views do not contain type information. They simply
define the raw data for retrieval from the file. Objects within the glTF
asset (meshes, skins, animations) access buffers or buffer views via
**accessors**.

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

##### 3.6.1.2. GLB-stored Buffer

<a href="#3612-glb-stored-buffer"
id="user-content-3612-glb-stored-buffer" class="anchor"
aria-label="Permalink: 3.6.1.2. GLB-stored Buffer"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

The glTF asset **MAY** use the GLB file container to pack glTF JSON and
one glTF buffer into one file. Data for such a buffer is provided via
the GLB-stored `BIN` chunk.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

A buffer with data provided by the GLB-stored `BIN` chunk, **MUST** be
the first element of `buffers` array and it **MUST** have its
`buffer.uri` property undefined. When such a buffer exists, a `BIN`
chunk **MUST** be present.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Any glTF buffer with undefined `buffer.uri` property that is not the
first element of `buffers` array does not refer to the GLB-stored BIN
chunk, and the behavior of such buffers is left undefined to accommodate
future extensions and specification versions.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

The byte length of the `BIN` chunk **MAY** be up to 3 bytes bigger than
JSON-defined `buffer.byteLength` value to satisfy GLB padding
requirements.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 50%" />
<col style="width: 50%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><div dir="auto">
Note
</div></td>
<td><div dir="auto">
Implementation Note
</div>
<div dir="auto">
<p>Not requiring strict equality of chunk’s and buffer’s lengths
slightly simplifies glTF to GLB conversion:
<code>buffer.byteLength</code> does not need to be updated after
applying GLB padding.</p>
</div></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

In the following example, the first buffer object refers to GLB-stored
data, while the second points to external resource:

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div dir="auto">

<div class="highlight highlight-source-json notranslate position-relative overflow-auto"
dir="auto" snippet-clipboard-copy-content="{
    &quot;buffers&quot;: [
        {
            &quot;byteLength&quot;: 35884
        },
        {
            &quot;byteLength&quot;: 504,
            &quot;uri&quot;: &quot;external.bin&quot;
        }
  ]
}">

    {
        "buffers": [
            {
                "byteLength": 35884
            },
            {
                "byteLength": 504,
                "uri": "external.bin"
            }
      ]
    }

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

See [GLB File Format Specification](#glb-file-format-specification) for
details on GLB File Format.

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

#### 3.6.2. Accessors

<a href="#362-accessors" id="user-content-362-accessors" class="anchor"
aria-label="Permalink: 3.6.2. Accessors"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

##### 3.6.2.1. Overview

<a href="#3621-overview" id="user-content-3621-overview" class="anchor"
aria-label="Permalink: 3.6.2.1. Overview"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

All binary data for meshes, skins, and animations is stored in buffers
and retrieved via accessors.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

An *accessor* defines a method for retrieving data as typed arrays from
within a buffer view. The accessor specifies a component type (e.g.,
*float*) and a data type (e.g., `VEC3` for 3D vectors), which when
combined define the complete data type for each data element. The number
of elements is specified using the `count` property. Elements could be,
e.g., vertex indices, vertex attributes, animation keyframes, etc.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

The `byteOffset` property specifies the location of the first data
element within the referenced buffer view. If the accessor is used for
vertex attributes (i.e., it is referenced by a mesh primitive or its
morph targets), the locations of the subsequent data elements are
controlled by the `bufferView.byteStride` property. If the accessor is
used for any other kind of data (vertex indices, animation keyframes,
etc.), its data elements are tightly packed.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

All accessors are stored in the asset’s `accessors` array.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

The following example shows two accessors, the first is a scalar
accessor for retrieving a primitive’s indices, and the second is a
3-float-component vector accessor for retrieving the primitive’s
position data.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div dir="auto">

<div class="highlight highlight-source-json notranslate position-relative overflow-auto"
dir="auto" snippet-clipboard-copy-content="{
    &quot;accessors&quot;: [
        {
            &quot;bufferView&quot;: 0,
            &quot;byteOffset&quot;: 0,
            &quot;componentType&quot;: 5123,
            &quot;count&quot;: 12636,
            &quot;max&quot;: [
                4212
            ],
            &quot;min&quot;: [
                0
            ],
            &quot;type&quot;: &quot;SCALAR&quot;
        },
        {
            &quot;bufferView&quot;: 1,
            &quot;byteOffset&quot;: 0,
            &quot;componentType&quot;: 5126,
            &quot;count&quot;: 2399,
            &quot;max&quot;: [
                0.961799,
                1.6397,
                0.539252
            ],
            &quot;min&quot;: [
                -0.692985,
                0.0992937,
                -0.613282
            ],
            &quot;type&quot;: &quot;VEC3&quot;
        }
    ]
}">

    {
        "accessors": [
            {
                "bufferView": 0,
                "byteOffset": 0,
                "componentType": 5123,
                "count": 12636,
                "max": [
                    4212
                ],
                "min": [
                    0
                ],
                "type": "SCALAR"
            },
            {
                "bufferView": 1,
                "byteOffset": 0,
                "componentType": 5126,
                "count": 2399,
                "max": [
                    0.961799,
                    1.6397,
                    0.539252
                ],
                "min": [
                    -0.692985,
                    0.0992937,
                    -0.613282
                ],
                "type": "VEC3"
            }
        ]
    }

</div>

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

##### 3.6.2.2. Accessor Data Types

<a href="#3622-accessor-data-types"
id="user-content-3622-accessor-data-types" class="anchor"
aria-label="Permalink: 3.6.2.2. Accessor Data Types"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

| `componentType` | Data Type        | Signed                   | Bits |
|-----------------|------------------|--------------------------|------|
| `5120`          | *signed byte*    | Signed, two’s complement | 8    |
| `5121`          | *unsigned byte*  | Unsigned                 | 8    |
| `5122`          | *signed short*   | Signed, two’s complement | 16   |
| `5123`          | *unsigned short* | Unsigned                 | 16   |
| `5125`          | *unsigned int*   | Unsigned                 | 32   |
| `5126`          | *float*          | Signed                   | 32   |

<div dir="auto">

Signed 32-bit integer components are not supported.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Floating-point data **MUST** use [IEEE-754](#ieee-754) single precision
format.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Values of `NaN`, `+Infinity`, and `-Infinity` **MUST NOT** be present.

</div>

| `type`     | Number of components |
|------------|----------------------|
| `"SCALAR"` | 1                    |
| `"VEC2"`   | 2                    |
| `"VEC3"`   | 3                    |
| `"VEC4"`   | 4                    |
| `"MAT2"`   | 4                    |
| `"MAT3"`   | 9                    |
| `"MAT4"`   | 16                   |

<div dir="auto">

Element size, in bytes, is
`(size in bytes of the 'componentType') * (number of components defined by 'type')`.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

For example:

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div dir="auto">

<div class="highlight highlight-source-json notranslate position-relative overflow-auto"
dir="auto" snippet-clipboard-copy-content="{
    &quot;accessors&quot;: [
        {
            &quot;bufferView&quot;: 1,
            &quot;byteOffset&quot;: 7032,
            &quot;componentType&quot;: 5126,
            &quot;count&quot;: 585,
            &quot;type&quot;: &quot;VEC3&quot;
        }
    ]
}">

    {
        "accessors": [
            {
                "bufferView": 1,
                "byteOffset": 7032,
                "componentType": 5126,
                "count": 585,
                "type": "VEC3"
            }
        ]
    }

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

In this accessor, the `componentType` is `5126` (*float*), so each
component is four bytes. The `type` is `"VEC3"`, so there are three
components. The size of each element is 12 bytes (`4 * 3`). Thus, the
accessor takes 7020 bytes (`[7032 …​ 14051]` inclusive range of the
buffer view).

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

##### 3.6.2.3. Sparse Accessors

<a href="#3623-sparse-accessors" id="user-content-3623-sparse-accessors"
class="anchor" aria-label="Permalink: 3.6.2.3. Sparse Accessors"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Sparse encoding of arrays is often more memory-efficient than dense
encoding when describing incremental changes with respect to a reference
array. This is often the case when encoding morph targets (it is, in
general, more efficient to describe a few displaced vertices in a morph
target than transmitting all morph target vertices).

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Similar to a standard accessor, a sparse accessor initializes an array
of typed elements from data stored in a `bufferView`. When
`accessor.bufferView` is undefined, the sparse accessor is initialized
as an array of zeros of size
`(size of the accessor element) * (accessor.count)` bytes.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

On top of that, a sparse accessor includes a `sparse` JSON object
describing the elements that are different from their initialization
values. The `sparse` object contains the following **REQUIRED**
properties:

</div>

<div dir="auto">

- `count`: number of displaced elements. This number **MUST NOT** be
  greater than the number of the base accessor elements.

- `indices`: object describing the location and the component type of
  indices of values to be replaced. The indices **MUST** form a strictly
  increasing sequence. The indices **MUST NOT** be greater than or equal
  to the number of the base accessor elements.

- `values`: object describing the location of displaced elements
  corresponding to the indices referred from the `indices`.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

The following example shows an example of a sparse accessor with 10
elements that are different from the initialization array.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div dir="auto">

<div class="highlight highlight-source-json notranslate position-relative overflow-auto"
dir="auto" snippet-clipboard-copy-content="{
    &quot;accessors&quot;: [
        {
            &quot;bufferView&quot;: 0,
            &quot;byteOffset&quot;: 0,
            &quot;componentType&quot;: 5123,
            &quot;count&quot;: 12636,
            &quot;type&quot;: &quot;VEC3&quot;,
            &quot;sparse&quot;: {
                &quot;count&quot;: 10,
                &quot;indices&quot;: {
                    &quot;bufferView&quot;: 1,
                    &quot;byteOffset&quot;: 0,
                    &quot;componentType&quot;: 5123
                },
                &quot;values&quot;: {
                    &quot;bufferView&quot;: 2,
                    &quot;byteOffset&quot;: 0
                }
            }
        }
    ]
}">

    {
        "accessors": [
            {
                "bufferView": 0,
                "byteOffset": 0,
                "componentType": 5123,
                "count": 12636,
                "type": "VEC3",
                "sparse": {
                    "count": 10,
                    "indices": {
                        "bufferView": 1,
                        "byteOffset": 0,
                        "componentType": 5123
                    },
                    "values": {
                        "bufferView": 2,
                        "byteOffset": 0
                    }
                }
            }
        ]
    }

</div>

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

##### 3.6.2.4. Data Alignment

<a href="#3624-data-alignment" id="user-content-3624-data-alignment"
class="anchor" aria-label="Permalink: 3.6.2.4. Data Alignment"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

The offset of an `accessor` into a `bufferView` (i.e.,
`accessor.byteOffset`) and the offset of an `accessor` into a `buffer`
(i.e., `accessor.byteOffset + bufferView.byteOffset`) **MUST** be a
multiple of the size of the accessor’s component type.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

When `byteStride` of the referenced `bufferView` is not defined, it
means that accessor elements are tightly packed, i.e., effective stride
equals the size of the element. When `byteStride` is defined, it
**MUST** be a multiple of the size of the accessor’s component type.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

When two or more vertex attribute accessors use the same `bufferView`,
its `byteStride` **MUST** be defined.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Each accessor **MUST** fit its `bufferView`, i.e.,

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div dir="auto">

<div class="snippet-clipboard-content notranslate position-relative overflow-auto"
snippet-clipboard-copy-content="accessor.byteOffset + EFFECTIVE_BYTE_STRIDE * (accessor.count - 1) + SIZE_OF_COMPONENT * NUMBER_OF_COMPONENTS">

``` notranslate
accessor.byteOffset + EFFECTIVE_BYTE_STRIDE * (accessor.count - 1) + SIZE_OF_COMPONENT * NUMBER_OF_COMPONENTS
```

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

**MUST** be less than or equal to `bufferView.length`.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

For performance and compatibility reasons, each element of a vertex
attribute **MUST** be aligned to 4-byte boundaries inside a `bufferView`
(i.e., `accessor.byteOffset` and `bufferView.byteStride` **MUST** be
multiples of 4).

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Accessors of matrix type have data stored in column-major order; start
of each column **MUST** be aligned to 4-byte boundaries. Specifically,
when `ROWS * SIZE_OF_COMPONENT` (where `ROWS` is the number of rows of
the matrix) is not a multiple of 4, then
`(ROWS * SIZE_OF_COMPONENT) % 4` padding bytes **MUST** be inserted at
the end of each column.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Only the following three accessor configurations require padding.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div dir="auto">

<a
href="/KhronosGroup/glTF/blob/main/specification/2.0/figures/padding-mat2-1byte.svg"
target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer"><img
src="/KhronosGroup/glTF/raw/main/specification/2.0/figures/padding-mat2-1byte.svg"
style="max-width: 100%;" alt="padding mat2 1byte" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Figure 3. Matrix 2x2, 1-byte Components

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div dir="auto">

<a
href="/KhronosGroup/glTF/blob/main/specification/2.0/figures/padding-mat3-1byte.svg"
target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer"><img
src="/KhronosGroup/glTF/raw/main/specification/2.0/figures/padding-mat3-1byte.svg"
style="max-width: 100%;" alt="padding mat3 1byte" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Figure 4. Matrix 3x3, 1-byte Components

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div dir="auto">

<a
href="/KhronosGroup/glTF/blob/main/specification/2.0/figures/padding-mat3-2byte.svg"
target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer"><img
src="/KhronosGroup/glTF/raw/main/specification/2.0/figures/padding-mat3-2byte.svg"
style="max-width: 100%;" alt="padding mat3 2byte" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Figure 5. Matrix 3x3, 2-byte Components

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Alignment requirements apply only to the start of each column, so
trailing bytes **MAY** be omitted if there’s no further data.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 50%" />
<col style="width: 50%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><div dir="auto">
Note
</div></td>
<td><div dir="auto">
Implementation Note
</div>
<div dir="auto">
<p>Alignment requirements allow client implementations to more
efficiently process binary buffers because creating aligned data views
usually does not require extra copying.</p>
</div></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Consider the following example:

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div dir="auto">

<div class="highlight highlight-source-json notranslate position-relative overflow-auto"
dir="auto" snippet-clipboard-copy-content="{
    &quot;bufferViews&quot;: [
        {
            &quot;buffer&quot;: 0,
            &quot;byteLength&quot;: 17136,
            &quot;byteOffset&quot;: 620
        }
    ],
    &quot;accessors&quot;: [
        {
            &quot;bufferView&quot;: 0,
            &quot;byteOffset&quot;: 4608,
            &quot;componentType&quot;: 5123,
            &quot;count&quot;: 42,
            &quot;type&quot;: &quot;VEC2&quot;
        }
    ]
}">

    {
        "bufferViews": [
            {
                "buffer": 0,
                "byteLength": 17136,
                "byteOffset": 620
            }
        ],
        "accessors": [
            {
                "bufferView": 0,
                "byteOffset": 4608,
                "componentType": 5123,
                "count": 42,
                "type": "VEC2"
            }
        ]
    }

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

In this example, the accessor describes tightly-packed two-component
unsigned short values.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

The corresponding segment of the underlying buffer would start from byte
5228

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div dir="auto">

<div class="snippet-clipboard-content notranslate position-relative overflow-auto"
snippet-clipboard-copy-content="start = accessor.byteOffset + accessor.bufferView.byteOffset">

``` notranslate
start = accessor.byteOffset + accessor.bufferView.byteOffset
```

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

and continue until byte 5396 exclusive

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div dir="auto">

<div class="snippet-clipboard-content notranslate position-relative overflow-auto"
snippet-clipboard-copy-content="end = 2 * 2 * accessor.count + start">

``` notranslate
end = 2 * 2 * accessor.count + start
```

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

The unsigned short view for the resulting buffer range could be created
without copying: 84 scalar values starting from byte offset 5228.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

When accessor values are not tightly-packed (i.e.,
`bufferView.byteStride` is greater than element’s byte length),
iteration over the created data view would need to take interleaved
values into account (i.e., skip them).

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

##### 3.6.2.5. Accessors Bounds

<a href="#3625-accessors-bounds" id="user-content-3625-accessors-bounds"
class="anchor" aria-label="Permalink: 3.6.2.5. Accessors Bounds"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

`accessor.min` and `accessor.max` properties are arrays that contain
per-component minimum and maximum values, respectively. The length of
these arrays **MUST** be equal to the number of accessor’s components.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Values stored in glTF JSON **MUST** match actual minimum and maximum
binary values stored in buffers. The `accessor.normalized` flag has no
effect on these properties.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

A sparse accessor `min` and `max` properties correspond, respectively,
to the minimum and maximum component values once the sparse substitution
is applied.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

When neither `sparse` nor `bufferView` is defined, `min` and `max`
properties **MAY** have any values. This is intended for use cases when
binary data is supplied by external means (e.g., via extensions).

</div>

<div dir="auto">

For floating-point components, JSON-stored minimum and maximum values
represent single precision floats and **SHOULD** be rounded to single
precision before usage to avoid any potential boundary mismatches.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 50%" />
<col style="width: 50%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><div dir="auto">
Note
</div></td>
<td><div dir="auto">
ECMAScript Implementation Note
</div>
<div dir="auto">
<p><code>Math.fround</code> function could be used to achieve that.</p>
</div></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Animation input and vertex position attribute accessors **MUST** have
`accessor.min` and `accessor.max` defined. For all other accessors,
these properties are optional.

</div>

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

### 3.7. Geometry

<a href="#37-geometry" id="user-content-37-geometry" class="anchor"
aria-label="Permalink: 3.7. Geometry"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

#### 3.7.1. Overview

<a href="#371-overview" id="user-content-371-overview" class="anchor"
aria-label="Permalink: 3.7.1. Overview"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Any node **MAY** contain one mesh, defined in its `mesh` property. The
mesh **MAY** be skinned using information provided in a referenced
`skin` object. The mesh **MAY** have morph targets.

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

#### 3.7.2. Meshes

<a href="#372-meshes" id="user-content-372-meshes" class="anchor"
aria-label="Permalink: 3.7.2. Meshes"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

##### 3.7.2.1. Overview

<a href="#3721-overview" id="user-content-3721-overview" class="anchor"
aria-label="Permalink: 3.7.2.1. Overview"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Meshes are defined as arrays of *primitives*. Primitives correspond to
the data required for GPU draw calls. Primitives specify one or more
`attributes`, corresponding to the vertex attributes used in the draw
calls. Indexed primitives also define an `indices` property. Attributes
and indices are defined as references to accessors containing
corresponding data. Each primitive **MAY** also specify a `material` and
a `mode` that corresponds to the GPU topology type (e.g., triangle set).

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 50%" />
<col style="width: 50%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><div dir="auto">
Note
</div></td>
<td><div dir="auto">
Implementation Note
</div>
<div dir="auto">
<p>Splitting one mesh into several <strong>primitives</strong> can be
useful to limit the number of indices per draw call or to assign
different materials to different parts of the mesh.</p>
</div></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

If `material` is undefined, then a [default material](#default-material)
**MUST** be used.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

The following example defines a mesh containing one indexed triangle
primitive:

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div dir="auto">

<div class="highlight highlight-source-json notranslate position-relative overflow-auto"
dir="auto" snippet-clipboard-copy-content="{
    &quot;meshes&quot;: [
        {
            &quot;primitives&quot;: [
                {
                    &quot;attributes&quot;: {
                        &quot;NORMAL&quot;: 23,
                        &quot;POSITION&quot;: 22,
                        &quot;TANGENT&quot;: 24,
                        &quot;TEXCOORD_0&quot;: 25
                    },
                    &quot;indices&quot;: 21,
                    &quot;material&quot;: 3,
                    &quot;mode&quot;: 4
                }
            ]
        }
    ]
}">

    {
        "meshes": [
            {
                "primitives": [
                    {
                        "attributes": {
                            "NORMAL": 23,
                            "POSITION": 22,
                            "TANGENT": 24,
                            "TEXCOORD_0": 25
                        },
                        "indices": 21,
                        "material": 3,
                        "mode": 4
                    }
                ]
            }
        ]
    }

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Each attribute is defined as a property of the `attributes` object. The
name of the property corresponds to an enumerated value identifying the
vertex attribute, such as `POSITION`. The value of the property is the
index of an accessor that contains the data.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

The specification defines the following attribute semantics: `POSITION`,
`NORMAL`, `TANGENT`, `TEXCOORD_n`, `COLOR_n`, `JOINTS_n`, and
`WEIGHTS_n`.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Application-specific attribute semantics **MUST** start with an
underscore, e.g., `_TEMPERATURE`. Application-specific attribute
semantics **MUST NOT** use *unsigned int* component type.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Valid accessor type and component type for each attribute semantic
property are defined below.

</div>

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 25%" />
<col style="width: 25%" />
<col style="width: 25%" />
<col style="width: 25%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Name</th>
<th>Accessor Type(s)</th>
<th>Component Type(s)</th>
<th>Description</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><p><code>POSITION</code></p></td>
<td><p>VEC3</p></td>
<td><p><em>float</em></p></td>
<td><p>Unitless XYZ vertex positions</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><p><code>NORMAL</code></p></td>
<td><p>VEC3</p></td>
<td><p><em>float</em></p></td>
<td><p>Normalized XYZ vertex normals</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><p><code>TANGENT</code></p></td>
<td><p>VEC4</p></td>
<td><p><em>float</em></p></td>
<td><p>XYZW vertex tangents where the XYZ portion is normalized, and the
W component is a sign value (-1 or +1) indicating handedness of the
tangent basis</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><p><code>TEXCOORD_n</code></p></td>
<td><p>VEC2</p></td>
<td><p><em>float</em><br />
<em>unsigned byte</em> normalized<br />
<em>unsigned short</em> normalized</p></td>
<td><p>ST texture coordinates</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><p><code>COLOR_n</code></p></td>
<td><p>VEC3<br />
VEC4</p></td>
<td><p><em>float</em><br />
<em>unsigned byte</em> normalized<br />
<em>unsigned short</em> normalized</p></td>
<td><p>RGB or RGBA vertex color linear multiplier</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><p><code>JOINTS_n</code></p></td>
<td><p>VEC4</p></td>
<td><p><em>unsigned byte</em> <em>unsigned short</em></p></td>
<td><p>See <a href="#skinned-mesh-attributes">Skinned Mesh
Attributes</a></p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><p><code>WEIGHTS_n</code></p></td>
<td><p>VEC4</p></td>
<td><p><em>float</em><br />
<em>unsigned byte</em> normalized<br />
<em>unsigned short</em> normalized</p></td>
<td><p>See <a href="#skinned-mesh-attributes">Skinned Mesh
Attributes</a></p></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

<div dir="auto">

`POSITION` accessor **MUST** have its `min` and `max` properties
defined.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

The W component of each `TANGENT` accessor element **MUST** be set to
`1.0` or `-1.0`.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

When a `COLOR_n` attribute uses an accessor of `"VEC3"` type, its alpha
component **MUST** be assumed to have a value of `1.0`.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

All components of each `COLOR_0` accessor element **MUST** be clamped to
`[0.0, 1.0]` range.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

`TEXCOORD_n`, `COLOR_n`, `JOINTS_n`, and `WEIGHTS_n` attribute semantic
property names **MUST** be of the form `[semantic]_[set_index]`, e.g.,
`TEXCOORD_0`, `TEXCOORD_1`, `COLOR_0`. All indices for indexed attribute
semantics **MUST** start with 0 and be consecutive positive integers:
`TEXCOORD_0`, `TEXCOORD_1`, etc. Indices **MUST NOT** use leading zeroes
to pad the number of digits (e.g., `TEXCOORD_01` is not allowed).

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Client implementations **SHOULD** support at least two texture
coordinate sets, one vertex color, and one joints/weights set.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

All attribute accessors for a given primitive **MUST** have the same
`count`. When `indices` property is not defined, attribute accessors'
`count` indicates the number of vertices to render; when `indices`
property is defined, it indicates the upper (exclusive) bound on the
index values in the `indices` accessor, i.e., all index values **MUST**
be less than attribute accessors' `count`.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

`indices` accessor **MUST NOT** contain the maximum possible value for
the component type used (i.e., 255 for unsigned bytes, 65535 for
unsigned shorts, 4294967295 for unsigned ints).

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 50%" />
<col style="width: 50%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><div dir="auto">
Note
</div></td>
<td><div dir="auto">
Implementation Note
</div>
<div dir="auto">
<p>The maximum values trigger primitive restart in some graphics APIs
and would require client implementations to rebuild the index
buffer.</p>
</div></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

When `indices` property is not defined, the number of vertex indices to
render is defined by `count` of attribute accessors (with the implied
values from range `[0..count)`); when `indices` property is defined, the
number of vertex indices to render is defined by `count` of accessor
referred to by `indices`. In either case, the number of vertex indices
**MUST** be valid for the topology type used:
