</div>

<div dir="auto">

- For *points*, it **MUST** be non-zero.

- For *line loops* and *line strips*, it **MUST** be 2 or greater.

- For *triangle strips* and *triangle fans*, it **MUST** be 3 or
  greater.

- For *lines*, it **MUST** be divisible by 2 and non-zero.

- For *triangles*, it **MUST** be divisible by 3 and non-zero

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Topology types are defined as follows.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

- **Points**

  <div dir="auto">

  Each vertex defines a single point primitive, according to the
  equation:

  </div>

  <div dir="auto">

    
  p<sub>i</sub> = {v<sub>i</sub>}

  </div>

- **Line Strips**

  <div dir="auto">

  One line primitive is defined by each vertex and the following vertex,
  according to the equation:

  </div>

  <div dir="auto">

    
  p<sub>i</sub> = {v<sub>i</sub>, v<sub>i+1</sub>}

  </div>

- **Line Loops**

  <div dir="auto">

  Loops are the same as line strips except that a final segment is added
  from the final specified vertex to the first vertex.

  </div>

- **Lines**

  <div dir="auto">

  Each consecutive pair of vertices defines a single line primitive,
  according to the equation:

  </div>

  <div dir="auto">

    
  p<sub>i</sub> = {v<sub>2i</sub>, v<sub>2i+1</sub>}

  </div>

- **Triangles**

  <div dir="auto">

  Each consecutive set of three vertices defines a single triangle
  primitive, according to the equation:

  </div>

  <div dir="auto">

    
  p<sub>i</sub> = {v<sub>3i</sub>, v<sub>3i+1</sub>, v<sub>3i+2</sub>}

  </div>

- **Triangle Strips**

  <div dir="auto">

  One triangle primitive is defined by each vertex and the two vertices
  that follow it, according to the equation:

  </div>

  <div dir="auto">

    
  p<sub>i</sub> = {v<sub>i</sub>, v<sub>i+(1+i%2)</sub>,
  v<sub>i+(2-i%2)</sub>}

  </div>

- **Triangle Fans**

  <div dir="auto">

  Triangle primitives are defined around a shared common vertex,
  according to the equation:

  </div>

  <div dir="auto">

    
  p<sub>i</sub> = {v<sub>i+1</sub>, v<sub>i+2</sub>, v<sub>0</sub>}

  </div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Mesh geometry **SHOULD NOT** contain degenerate lines or triangles,
i.e., lines or triangles that use the same vertex more than once per
topology primitive.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

When positions are not specified, client implementations **SHOULD** skip
primitive’s rendering unless its positions are provided by other means
(e.g., by an extension). This applies to both indexed and non-indexed
geometry.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

When tangents are not specified, client implementations **SHOULD**
calculate tangents using default [MikkTSpace](#mikktspace) algorithms
with the specified vertex positions, normals, and texture coordinates
associated with the normal texture.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

When normals are not specified, client implementations **MUST**
calculate flat normals and the provided tangents (if present) **MUST**
be ignored.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Vertices of the same triangle **SHOULD** have the same `tangent.w`
value. When vertices of the same triangle have different `tangent.w`
values, its tangent space is considered undefined.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

The bitangent vectors **MUST** be computed by taking the cross product
of the normal and tangent XYZ vectors and multiplying it against the W
component of the tangent:
`bitangent = cross(normal.xyz, tangent.xyz) * tangent.w`.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Extensions **MAY** add additional attribute names, accessor types,
and/or component types.

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

##### 3.7.2.2. Morph Targets

<a href="#3722-morph-targets" id="user-content-3722-morph-targets"
class="anchor" aria-label="Permalink: 3.7.2.2. Morph Targets"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Morph targets are defined by extending the Mesh concept.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

A morph target is a morphable Mesh where the primitives' attributes are
obtained by adding the original attributes to a weighted sum of the
target’s attributes.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

For instance, the morph target vertices `POSITION` for the primitive at
index **i** are computed in this way:

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div dir="auto">

<div class="highlight highlight-source-c notranslate position-relative overflow-auto"
dir="auto"
snippet-clipboard-copy-content="primitives[i].attributes.POSITION +
  weights[0] * primitives[i].targets[0].POSITION +
  weights[1] * primitives[i].targets[1].POSITION +
  weights[2] * primitives[i].targets[2].POSITION + ...">

    primitives[i].attributes.POSITION +
      weights[0] * primitives[i].targets[0].POSITION +
      weights[1] * primitives[i].targets[1].POSITION +
      weights[2] * primitives[i].targets[2].POSITION + ...

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Morph targets are specified via the `targets` property defined in the
Mesh `primitives`. Each target in the `targets` array is a plain JSON
object mapping a primitive attribute to an accessor containing morph
target displacement data (deltas).

</div>

<div dir="auto">

For each morph target attribute, an original attribute **MUST** be
present in the mesh primitive.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Attributes present in the base mesh primitive but not included in a
given morph target **MUST** retain their original values for the morph
target.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 50%" />
<col style="width: 50%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><div dir="auto">
Note
</div></td>
<td><div dir="auto">
Implementation Note
</div>
<div dir="auto">
<p>This allows skipping zero-filled accessors and implies that different
morph targets may contain different sets of attributes.</p>
</div></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Client implementations **SHOULD** support at least three
attributes — `POSITION`, `NORMAL`, and `TANGENT` — for morphing. Client
implementations **MAY** optionally support morphed `TEXCOORD_n` and/or
`COLOR_n` attributes.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

If morph targets contain application-specific semantics, their names
**MUST** be prefixed with an underscore (e.g., `_TEMPERATURE`) like the
associated attribute semantics.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

All primitives **MUST** have the same number of morph targets in the
same order.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Accessor type and component type for each morphed attribute semantic
property **MUST** follow the table below. Note that the W component for
handedness is omitted when targeting `TANGENT` data since handedness
cannot be displaced.

</div>

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 25%" />
<col style="width: 25%" />
<col style="width: 25%" />
<col style="width: 25%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Name</th>
<th>Accessor Type(s)</th>
<th>Component Type(s)</th>
<th>Description</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><p><code>POSITION</code></p></td>
<td><p>VEC3</p></td>
<td><p><em>float</em></p></td>
<td><p>XYZ vertex position displacements</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><p><code>NORMAL</code></p></td>
<td><p>VEC3</p></td>
<td><p><em>float</em></p></td>
<td><p>XYZ vertex normal displacements</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><p><code>TANGENT</code></p></td>
<td><p>VEC3</p></td>
<td><p><em>float</em></p></td>
<td><p>XYZ vertex tangent displacements</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><p><code>TEXCOORD_n</code></p></td>
<td><p>VEC2</p></td>
<td><p><em>float</em><br />
<em>signed byte</em> normalized<br />
<em>signed short</em> normalized<br />
<em>unsigned byte</em> normalized<br />
<em>unsigned short</em> normalized</p></td>
<td><p>ST texture coordinate displacements</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><p><code>COLOR_n</code></p></td>
<td><p>VEC3<br />
VEC4</p></td>
<td><p><em>float</em><br />
<em>signed byte</em> normalized<br />
<em>signed short</em> normalized<br />
<em>unsigned byte</em> normalized<br />
<em>unsigned short</em> normalized</p></td>
<td><p>RGB or RGBA color deltas</p></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

<div dir="auto">

`POSITION` accessor **MUST** have its `min` and `max` properties
defined.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Displacements for `POSITION`, `NORMAL`, and `TANGENT` attributes
**MUST** be applied before any transformation matrices affecting the
mesh vertices such as skinning or node transforms.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

When the base mesh primitive does not specify tangents, client
implementations **SHOULD** calculate tangents for each morph target
using default [MikkTSpace](#mikktspace) algorithms with the updated
vertex positions, normals, and texture coordinates associated with the
normal texture.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

When the base mesh primitive does not specify normals, client
implementations **MUST** calculate flat normals for each morph target;
the provided tangents and their displacements (if present) **MUST** be
ignored.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

When `COLOR_n` deltas use an accessor of `"VEC3"` type, their alpha
components **MUST** be assumed to have a value of `0.0`.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

After applying color deltas, all components of each `COLOR_0` morphed
accessor element **MUST** be clamped to `[0.0, 1.0]` range.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

All morph target accessors **MUST** have the same `count` as the
accessors of the original primitive.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

A mesh with morph targets **MAY** also define an optional `mesh.weights`
property that stores the default targets' weights. These weights
**MUST** be used when `node.weights` is undefined. When `mesh.weights`
is undefined, the default targets' weights are zeros.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

The following example extends the Mesh defined in the previous example
to a morphable one by adding two morph targets:

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div dir="auto">

<div class="highlight highlight-source-json notranslate position-relative overflow-auto"
dir="auto" snippet-clipboard-copy-content="{
    &quot;primitives&quot;: [
        {
            &quot;attributes&quot;: {
                &quot;NORMAL&quot;: 23,
                &quot;POSITION&quot;: 22,
                &quot;TANGENT&quot;: 24,
                &quot;TEXCOORD_0&quot;: 25
            },
            &quot;indices&quot;: 21,
            &quot;material&quot;: 3,
            &quot;targets&quot;: [
                {
                    &quot;NORMAL&quot;: 33,
                    &quot;POSITION&quot;: 32,
                    &quot;TANGENT&quot;: 34
                },
                {
                    &quot;NORMAL&quot;: 43,
                    &quot;POSITION&quot;: 42,
                    &quot;TANGENT&quot;: 44
                }
            ]
        }
    ],
    &quot;weights&quot;: [0, 0.5]
}">

    {
        "primitives": [
            {
                "attributes": {
                    "NORMAL": 23,
                    "POSITION": 22,
                    "TANGENT": 24,
                    "TEXCOORD_0": 25
                },
                "indices": 21,
                "material": 3,
                "targets": [
                    {
                        "NORMAL": 33,
                        "POSITION": 32,
                        "TANGENT": 34
                    },
                    {
                        "NORMAL": 43,
                        "POSITION": 42,
                        "TANGENT": 44
                    }
                ]
            }
        ],
        "weights": [0, 0.5]
    }

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

The number of morph targets is not limited. Client implementations
**SHOULD** support at least eight morphed attributes. This means that
they **SHOULD** support eight morph targets when each morph target has
one attribute, four morph targets where each morph target has two
attributes, or two morph targets where each morph target has three or
four attributes.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

For assets that contain a higher number of morphed attributes, client
implementations **MAY** choose to only use the eight attributes of the
morph targets with the highest weights.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 50%" />
<col style="width: 50%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><div dir="auto">
Note
</div></td>
<td><div dir="auto">
Implementation Note
</div>
<div dir="auto">
<p>A significant number of authoring and client implementations
associate names with morph targets. While the glTF 2.0 specification
currently does not provide a way to specify names, most tools use an
array of strings, <code>mesh.extras.targetNames</code>, for this
purpose. The <code>targetNames</code> array and all primitive
<code>targets</code> arrays must have the same length.</p>
</div></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

#### 3.7.3. Skins

<a href="#373-skins" id="user-content-373-skins" class="anchor"
aria-label="Permalink: 3.7.3. Skins"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

##### 3.7.3.1. Overview

<a href="#3731-overview" id="user-content-3731-overview" class="anchor"
aria-label="Permalink: 3.7.3.1. Overview"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

glTF 2.0 meshes support Linear Blend Skinning via skin objects, joint
hierarchies, and designated vertex attributes.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Skins are stored in the `skins` array of the asset. Each skin is defined
by a **REQUIRED** `joints` property that lists the indices of nodes used
as joints to pose the skin and an **OPTIONAL** `inverseBindMatrices`
property that points to an accessor with inverse bind matrices data used
to bring coordinates being skinned into the same space as each joint.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

The order of joints is defined by the `skin.joints` array and it
**MUST** match the order of `inverseBindMatrices` accessor elements
(when the latter is present). The `skeleton` property (if present)
points to the node that is the common root of a joints hierarchy or to a
direct or indirect parent node of the common root.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 50%" />
<col style="width: 50%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><div dir="auto">
Note
</div></td>
<td><div dir="auto">
Implementation Note
</div>
<div dir="auto">
<p>Although the <code>skeleton</code> property is not needed for
computing skinning transforms, it may be used to provide a specific
“pivot point” for the skinned geometry.</p>
</div></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

An accessor referenced by `inverseBindMatrices` **MUST** have
floating-point components of `"MAT4"` type. The number of elements of
the accessor referenced by `inverseBindMatrices` **MUST** be greater
than or equal to the number of `joints` elements. The fourth row of each
matrix **MUST** be set to `[0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0]`.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 50%" />
<col style="width: 50%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><div dir="auto">
Note
</div></td>
<td><div dir="auto">
Implementation Note
</div>
<div dir="auto">
<p>The matrix defining how to pose the skin’s geometry for use with the
joints (also known as “Bind Shape Matrix”) should be premultiplied to
mesh data or to Inverse Bind Matrices.</p>
</div></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

##### 3.7.3.2. Joint Hierarchy

<a href="#3732-joint-hierarchy" id="user-content-3732-joint-hierarchy"
class="anchor" aria-label="Permalink: 3.7.3.2. Joint Hierarchy"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

The joint hierarchy used for controlling skinned mesh pose is simply the
node hierarchy, with each node designated as a *joint* by a reference
from the `skin.joints` array. Each skin’s joints **MUST** have a common
parent node (direct or indirect) called *common root*, which may or may
not be a joint node itself. When a skin is referenced by a node within a
scene, the common root **MUST** belong to the same scene.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 50%" />
<col style="width: 50%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><div dir="auto">
Note
</div></td>
<td><div dir="auto">
Implementation Note
</div>
<div dir="auto">
<p>A node object does not specify whether it is a joint. Client
implementations may need to traverse the <code>skins</code> array first,
marking each joint node.</p>
</div></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

A joint node **MAY** have other nodes attached to it, even a complete
node sub graph with meshes.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 50%" />
<col style="width: 50%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><div dir="auto">
Note
</div></td>
<td><div dir="auto">
Implementation Note
</div>
<div dir="auto">
<p>It’s common to have an entire geometry attached to a joint node
without having it being skinned (e.g., a sword attached to a hand). Note
that the node transform is the local transform of the node relative to
the joint, like any other node in the glTF node hierarchy as described
in the <a href="#transformations">Transformations</a> section.</p>
</div></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Only the joint transforms are applied to the skinned mesh; the transform
of the skinned mesh node **MUST** be ignored.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

In the example below, the translation of `node_0` and the scale of
`node_1` are applied while the translation of `node_3` and rotation of
`node_4` are ignored.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div dir="auto">

<div class="highlight highlight-source-json notranslate position-relative overflow-auto"
dir="auto" snippet-clipboard-copy-content="{
    &quot;nodes&quot;: [
        {
            &quot;name&quot;: &quot;node_0&quot;,
            &quot;children&quot;: [ 1 ],
            &quot;translation&quot;: [ 0.0, 1.0, 0.0 ]
        },
        {
            &quot;name&quot;: &quot;node_1&quot;,
            &quot;children&quot;: [ 2 ],
            &quot;scale&quot;: [ 0.5, 0.5, 0.5 ]
        },
        {
            &quot;name&quot;: &quot;node_2&quot;
        },
        {
            &quot;name&quot;: &quot;node_3&quot;,
            &quot;children&quot;: [ 4 ],
            &quot;translation&quot;: [ 1.0, 0.0, 0.0 ]
        },
        {
            &quot;name&quot;: &quot;node_4&quot;,
            &quot;mesh&quot;: 0,
            &quot;rotation&quot;: [ 0.0, 1.0, 0.0, 0.0 ],
            &quot;skin&quot;: 0
        }
    ],
    &quot;skins&quot;: [
        {
            &quot;inverseBindMatrices&quot;: 0,
            &quot;joints&quot;: [ 1, 2 ],
            &quot;skeleton&quot;: 1
        }
    ]
}">

    {
        "nodes": [
            {
                "name": "node_0",
                "children": [ 1 ],
                "translation": [ 0.0, 1.0, 0.0 ]
            },
            {
                "name": "node_1",
                "children": [ 2 ],
                "scale": [ 0.5, 0.5, 0.5 ]
            },
            {
                "name": "node_2"
            },
            {
                "name": "node_3",
                "children": [ 4 ],
                "translation": [ 1.0, 0.0, 0.0 ]
            },
            {
                "name": "node_4",
                "mesh": 0,
                "rotation": [ 0.0, 1.0, 0.0, 0.0 ],
                "skin": 0
            }
        ],
        "skins": [
            {
                "inverseBindMatrices": 0,
                "joints": [ 1, 2 ],
                "skeleton": 1
            }
        ]
    }

</div>

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

##### 3.7.3.3. Skinned Mesh Attributes

<a href="#3733-skinned-mesh-attributes"
id="user-content-3733-skinned-mesh-attributes" class="anchor"
aria-label="Permalink: 3.7.3.3. Skinned Mesh Attributes"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

The skinned mesh **MUST** have vertex attributes that are used in
skinning calculations. The `JOINTS_n` attribute data contains the
indices of the joints from the corresponding `skin.joints` array that
affect the vertex. The `WEIGHTS_n` attribute data defines the weights
indicating how strongly the joint influences the vertex.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

To apply skinning, a transformation matrix is computed for each joint.
Then, the per-vertex transformation matrices are computed as weighted
linear sums of the joint transformation matrices. Note that per-joint
inverse bind matrices (when present) **MUST** be applied before the base
node transforms.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

In the following example, a mesh primitive defines `JOINTS_0` and
`WEIGHTS_0` vertex attributes:

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div dir="auto">

<div class="highlight highlight-source-json notranslate position-relative overflow-auto"
dir="auto" snippet-clipboard-copy-content="{
    &quot;meshes&quot;: [
        {
            &quot;name&quot;: &quot;skinned-mesh_1&quot;,
            &quot;primitives&quot;: [
                {
                    &quot;attributes&quot;: {
                        &quot;JOINTS_0&quot;: 179,
                        &quot;NORMAL&quot;: 165,
                        &quot;POSITION&quot;: 163,
                        &quot;TEXCOORD_0&quot;: 167,
                        &quot;WEIGHTS_0&quot;: 176
                    },
                    &quot;indices&quot;: 161,
                    &quot;material&quot;: 1,
                    &quot;mode&quot;: 4
                }
            ]
        }
    ]
}">

    {
        "meshes": [
            {
                "name": "skinned-mesh_1",
                "primitives": [
                    {
                        "attributes": {
                            "JOINTS_0": 179,
                            "NORMAL": 165,
                            "POSITION": 163,
                            "TEXCOORD_0": 167,
                            "WEIGHTS_0": 176
                        },
                        "indices": 161,
                        "material": 1,
                        "mode": 4
                    }
                ]
            }
        ]
    }

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

The number of joints that influence one vertex is limited to 4 per set,
so the referenced accessors **MUST** have `VEC4` type and following
component types:

</div>

<div dir="auto">

- **`JOINTS_n`**: *unsigned byte* or *unsigned short*

- **`WEIGHTS_n`**: *float*, or *normalized unsigned byte*, or
  *normalized unsigned short*

</div>

<div dir="auto">

The joint weights for each vertex **MUST NOT** be negative.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Joints **MUST NOT** contain more than one non-zero weight for a given
vertex.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

When the weights are stored using *float* component type, their linear
sum **SHOULD** be as close as reasonably possible to `1.0` for a given
vertex.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

When the weights are stored using *normalized unsigned byte*, or
*normalized unsigned short* component types, their linear sum before
normalization **MUST** be `255` or `65535` respectively. Without these
requirements, vertices would be deformed significantly because the
weight error would get multiplied by the joint position. For example, an
error of `1/255` in the weight sum would result in an unacceptably large
difference in the joint position.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 50%" />
<col style="width: 50%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><div dir="auto">
Note
</div></td>
<td><div dir="auto">
Implementation Note
</div>
<div dir="auto">
<p>The threshold in the official validation tool is set to
<code>2e-7</code> times the number of non-zero weights per vertex.</p>
</div></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 50%" />
<col style="width: 50%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><div dir="auto">
Note
</div></td>
<td><div dir="auto">
Implementation Note
</div>
<div dir="auto">
<p>Since the allowed threshold is much lower than minimum possible step
for quantized component types, weight sum should be renormalized after
quantization.</p>
</div></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

When any of the vertices are influenced by more than four joints, the
additional joint and weight information are stored in subsequent sets.
For example, `JOINTS_1` and `WEIGHTS_1` if present will reference the
accessor for up to 4 additional joints that influence the vertices. For
a given primitive, the number of `JOINTS_n` attribute sets **MUST** be
equal to the number of `WEIGHTS_n` attribute sets.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Client implementations **MAY** support only a single set of up to four
weights and joints, however not supporting all weight and joint sets
present in the file may have an impact on the asset’s animation.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

All joint values **MUST** be within the range of joints in the skin.
Unused joint values (i.e., joints with a weight of zero) **SHOULD** be
set to zero.

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

#### 3.7.4. Instantiation

<a href="#374-instantiation" id="user-content-374-instantiation"
class="anchor" aria-label="Permalink: 3.7.4. Instantiation"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

A mesh is instantiated by `node.mesh` property. The same mesh could be
used by many nodes, which could have different transforms. For example:

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div dir="auto">

<div class="highlight highlight-source-json notranslate position-relative overflow-auto"
dir="auto" snippet-clipboard-copy-content="{
    &quot;nodes&quot;: [
        {
            &quot;mesh&quot;: 11
        },
        {
            &quot;mesh&quot;: 11,
            &quot;translation&quot;: [
                -20,
                -1,
                0
            ]
        }
    ]
}">

    {
        "nodes": [
            {
                "mesh": 11
            },
            {
                "mesh": 11,
                "translation": [
                    -20,
                    -1,
                    0
                ]
            }
        ]
    }

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

After applying the node’s global transform, mesh vertex position values
are meters.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

When a mesh primitive uses any triangle-based topology (i.e.,
*triangles*, *triangle strip*, or *triangle fan*), the determinant of
the node’s global transform defines the winding order of that primitive.
If the determinant is a positive value, the winding order triangle faces
is counterclockwise; in the opposite case, the winding order is
clockwise.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 50%" />
<col style="width: 50%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><div dir="auto">
Note
</div></td>
<td><div dir="auto">
Implementation Note
</div>
<div dir="auto">
<p>Switching the winding order to clockwise enables mirroring geometry
via negative scale transforms.</p>
</div></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

When an instantiated mesh has morph targets, it **MUST** use morph
weights specified with the `node.weights` property. When the latter is
undefined, `mesh.weights` property **MUST** be used instead. When both
of these fields are undefined, the mesh is instantiated in a non-morphed
state (i.e., with all morph weights set to zeros).

</div>

<div dir="auto">

The example below instantiates a Morph Target with non-default weights.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div dir="auto">

<div class="highlight highlight-source-json notranslate position-relative overflow-auto"
dir="auto" snippet-clipboard-copy-content="{
    &quot;nodes&quot;: [
        {
            &quot;mesh&quot;: 11,
            &quot;weights&quot;: [0, 0.5]
        }
    ]
}">

    {
        "nodes": [
            {
                "mesh": 11,
                "weights": [0, 0.5]
            }
        ]
    }

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

A skin is instantiated within a node using a combination of the node’s
`mesh` and `skin` properties. The mesh for a skin instance is defined in
the `mesh` property. The `skin` property contains the index of the skin
to instance.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

The following example shows a skinned mesh instance: a skin object, a
node with a skinned mesh, and two joint nodes.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div dir="auto">

<div class="highlight highlight-source-json notranslate position-relative overflow-auto"
dir="auto" snippet-clipboard-copy-content="{
    &quot;skins&quot;: [
        {
            &quot;inverseBindMatrices&quot;: 29,
            &quot;joints&quot;: [1, 2]
        }
    ],
    &quot;nodes&quot;: [
        {
            &quot;name&quot;:&quot;Skinned mesh node&quot;,
            &quot;mesh&quot;: 0,
            &quot;skin&quot;: 0
        },
        {
            &quot;name&quot;:&quot;Skeleton root joint&quot;,
            &quot;children&quot;: [2],
            &quot;rotation&quot;: [
                0,
                0,
                0.7071067811865475,
                0.7071067811865476
            ],
            &quot;translation&quot;: [
                4.61599,
                -2.032e-06,
                -5.08e-08
            ]
        },
        {
            &quot;name&quot;:&quot;Head&quot;,
            &quot;translation&quot;: [
                8.76635,
                0,
                0
            ]
        }
    ]
}">

    {
        "skins": [
            {
                "inverseBindMatrices": 29,
                "joints": [1, 2]
            }
        ],
        "nodes": [
            {
                "name":"Skinned mesh node",
                "mesh": 0,
                "skin": 0
            },
            {
                "name":"Skeleton root joint",
                "children": [2],
                "rotation": [
                    0,
                    0,
                    0.7071067811865475,
                    0.7071067811865476
                ],
                "translation": [
                    4.61599,
                    -2.032e-06,
                    -5.08e-08
                ]
            },
            {
                "name":"Head",
                "translation": [
                    8.76635,
                    0,
                    0
                ]
            }
        ]
    }

</div>

</div>

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

### 3.8. Texture Data

<a href="#38-texture-data" id="user-content-38-texture-data"
class="anchor" aria-label="Permalink: 3.8. Texture Data"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

#### 3.8.1. Overview

<a href="#381-overview" id="user-content-381-overview" class="anchor"
aria-label="Permalink: 3.8.1. Overview"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

glTF 2.0 separates texture access into three distinct types of objects:
Textures, Images, and Samplers.

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

#### 3.8.2. Textures

<a href="#382-textures" id="user-content-382-textures" class="anchor"
aria-label="Permalink: 3.8.2. Textures"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Textures are stored in the asset’s `textures` array. A texture is
defined by an image index, denoted by the `source` property and a
sampler index (`sampler`). For example:

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div dir="auto">

<div class="highlight highlight-source-json notranslate position-relative overflow-auto"
dir="auto" snippet-clipboard-copy-content="{
    &quot;textures&quot;: [
        {
            &quot;sampler&quot;: 0,
            &quot;source&quot;: 2
        }
    ]
}">

    {
        "textures": [
            {
                "sampler": 0,
                "source": 2
            }
        ]
    }

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

glTF 2.0 supports only static 2D textures.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

When `texture.source` is undefined, the image **SHOULD** be provided by
an extension or application-specific means, otherwise the texture object
is undefined.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 50%" />
<col style="width: 50%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><div dir="auto">
Note
</div></td>
<td><div dir="auto">
Implementation Note
</div>
<div dir="auto">
<p>Client implementations may render such textures with a predefined
placeholder image or being filled with some error color (usually
magenta).</p>
</div></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

When `texture.sampler` is undefined, a sampler with repeat wrapping (in
both directions) and auto filtering **MUST** be used.

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

#### 3.8.3. Images

<a href="#383-images" id="user-content-383-images" class="anchor"
aria-label="Permalink: 3.8.3. Images"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Images referred to by textures are stored in the `images` array of the
asset.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Each image contains one of

</div>

<div dir="auto">

- a URI (or IRI) to an external file in one of the supported image
  formats, or

- a Data URI with embedded data, or

- a reference to a `bufferView`; in that case `mimeType` **MUST** be
  defined.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

The following example shows an image pointing to an external PNG image
file and another image referencing a `bufferView` with JPEG data.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div dir="auto">

<div class="highlight highlight-source-json notranslate position-relative overflow-auto"
dir="auto" snippet-clipboard-copy-content="{
    &quot;images&quot;: [
        {
            &quot;uri&quot;: &quot;duckCM.png&quot;
        },
        {
            &quot;bufferView&quot;: 14,
            &quot;mimeType&quot;: &quot;image/jpeg&quot;
        }
    ]
}">

    {
        "images": [
            {
                "uri": "duckCM.png"
            },
            {
                "bufferView": 14,
                "mimeType": "image/jpeg"
            }
        ]
    }

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Client implementations **MAY** need to manually determine the media type
of some images. In such a case, the following table **SHOULD** be used
to check the values of the first few bytes.

</div>

| Media Type   | Pattern Length | Pattern Bytes                             |
|--------------|----------------|-------------------------------------------|
| `image/png`  | 8              | `0x89 0x50 0x4E 0x47 0x0D 0x0A 0x1A 0x0A` |
| `image/jpeg` | 3              | `0xFF 0xD8 0xFF`                          |

<div dir="auto">

The image data **MUST** match the `image.mimeType` property when the
latter is defined.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

The origin of the texture coordinates (0, 0) corresponds to the upper
left corner of a texture image. This is illustrated in the following
figure, where the respective coordinates are shown for all four corners
of a normalized texture space:

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div dir="auto">

<a
href="/KhronosGroup/glTF/blob/main/specification/2.0/figures/texcoords.svg"
target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer"><img
src="/KhronosGroup/glTF/raw/main/specification/2.0/figures/texcoords.svg"
style="max-width: 100%;" alt="texcoords" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Figure 6. Normalized Texture Coordinates

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Any colorspace information (such as ICC profiles, intents, gamma values,
etc.) from PNG or JPEG images **MUST** be ignored. Effective transfer
function (encoding) is defined by a glTF object that refers to the image
(in most cases it’s a texture that is used by a material).

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 50%" />
<col style="width: 50%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><div dir="auto">
Note
</div></td>
<td><div dir="auto">
Web Implementation Note
</div>
<div dir="auto">
<p>To ignore embedded colorspace information when using WebGL API, set
<code>UNPACK_COLORSPACE_CONVERSION_WEBGL</code> flag to
<code>NONE</code>.</p>
</div>
<div dir="auto">
<p>To ignore embedded colorspace information when using ImageBitmap API,
set <code>colorSpaceConversion</code> option to <code>none</code>.</p>
</div></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

#### 3.8.4. Samplers

<a href="#384-samplers" id="user-content-384-samplers" class="anchor"
aria-label="Permalink: 3.8.4. Samplers"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

##### 3.8.4.1. Overview

<a href="#3841-overview" id="user-content-3841-overview" class="anchor"
aria-label="Permalink: 3.8.4.1. Overview"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Samplers are stored in the `samplers` array of the asset. Each sampler
specifies filtering and wrapping modes.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

The sampler properties use integer enums defined in the [Properties
Reference](#reference-sampler).

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Client implementations **SHOULD** follow specified filtering modes. When
the latter are undefined, client implementations **MAY** set their own
default texture filtering settings.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Client implementations **MUST** follow specified wrapping modes.

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

##### 3.8.4.2. Filtering

<a href="#3842-filtering" id="user-content-3842-filtering"
class="anchor" aria-label="Permalink: 3.8.4.2. Filtering"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Filtering modes control texture’s magnification and minification.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Magnification modes include:

</div>

<div dir="auto">

- *Nearest*. For each requested texel coordinate, the sampler selects a
  texel with the nearest coordinates. This process is sometimes called
  “nearest neighbor”.

- *Linear*. For each requested texel coordinate, the sampler computes a
  weighted sum of several adjacent texels. This process is sometimes
  called “bilinear interpolation”.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Minification modes include:

</div>

<div dir="auto">

- *Nearest*. For each requested texel coordinate, the sampler selects a
  texel with the nearest (in Manhattan distance) coordinates from the
  original image. This process is sometimes called “nearest neighbor”.

- *Linear*. For each requested texel coordinate, the sampler computes a
  weighted sum of several adjacent texels from the original image. This
  process is sometimes called “bilinear interpolation”.

- *Nearest-mipmap-nearest*. For each requested texel coordinate, the
  sampler first selects one of pre-minified versions of the original
  image, and then selects a texel with the nearest (in Manhattan
  distance) coordinates from it.

- *Linear-mipmap-nearest*. For each requested texel coordinate, the
  sampler first selects one of pre-minified versions of the original
  image, and then computes a weighted sum of several adjacent texels
  from it.

- *Nearest-mipmap-linear*. For each requested texel coordinate, the
  sampler first selects two pre-minified versions of the original image,
  selects a texel with the nearest (in Manhattan distance) coordinates
  from each of them, and performs final linear interpolation between
  these two intermediate results.

- *Linear-mipmap-linear*. For each requested texel coordinate, the
  sampler first selects two pre-minified versions of the original image,
  computes a weighted sum of several adjacent texels from each of them,
  and performs final linear interpolation between these two intermediate
  results. This process is sometimes called “trilinear interpolation”.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

To properly support mipmap modes, client implementations **SHOULD**
generate mipmaps at runtime. When runtime mipmap generation is not
possible, client implementations **SHOULD** override the minification
filtering mode as follows:

</div>

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 50%" />
<col style="width: 50%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Mipmap minification mode</th>
<th>Fallback mode</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><p><em>Nearest-mipmap-nearest</em><br />
<em>Nearest-mipmap-linear</em></p></td>
<td><p><em>Nearest</em></p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><p><em>Linear-mipmap-nearest</em><br />
<em>Linear-mipmap-linear</em></p></td>
<td><p><em>Linear</em></p></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

##### 3.8.4.3. Wrapping

<a href="#3843-wrapping" id="user-content-3843-wrapping" class="anchor"
aria-label="Permalink: 3.8.4.3. Wrapping"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Per-vertex texture coordinates, which are provided via `TEXCOORD_n`
attribute values, are normalized for the image size (not to confuse with
the `normalized` accessor property, the latter refers only to data
encoding). That is, the texture coordinate value of `(0.0, 0.0)` points
to the beginning of the first (upper-left) image pixel, while the
texture coordinate value of `(1.0, 1.0)` points to the end of the last
(lower-right) image pixel.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Sampler’s wrapping modes define how to handle texture coordinates that
are negative or greater than or equal to `1.0`, independently for both
directions. Supported modes include:

</div>

<div dir="auto">

- *Repeat*. Only the fractional part of texture coordinates is used.

  <div dir="auto">

  <table>
  <colgroup>
  <col style="width: 50%" />
  <col style="width: 50%" />
  </colgroup>
  <tbody>
  <tr>
  <td><div dir="auto">
  Note
  </div></td>
  <td><div dir="auto">
  Example
  </div>
  <div dir="auto">
  <p><code>2.2</code> maps to <code>0.2</code>; <code>-0.4</code> maps to
  <code>0.6</code>.</p>
  </div></td>
  </tr>
  </tbody>
  </table>

  </div>

- *Mirrored Repeat*. This mode works as *repeat* but flips the direction
  when the integer part (truncated towards −∞) is odd.

  <div dir="auto">

  <table>
  <colgroup>
  <col style="width: 50%" />
  <col style="width: 50%" />
  </colgroup>
  <tbody>
  <tr>
  <td><div dir="auto">
  Note
  </div></td>
  <td><div dir="auto">
  Example
  </div>
  <div dir="auto">
  <p><code>2.2</code> maps to <code>0.2</code>; <code>-0.4</code> is
  treated as <code>0.4</code>.</p>
  </div></td>
  </tr>
  </tbody>
  </table>

  </div>

- *Clamp to edge*. Texture coordinates with values outside the image are
  clamped to the closest existing image texel at the edge.

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

##### 3.8.4.4. Example

<a href="#3844-example" id="user-content-3844-example" class="anchor"
aria-label="Permalink: 3.8.4.4. Example"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

The following example defines a sampler with *linear* magnification
filtering, *linear-mipmap-linear* minification filtering, and *repeat*
wrapping in both directions.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div dir="auto">

<div class="highlight highlight-source-json notranslate position-relative overflow-auto"
dir="auto" snippet-clipboard-copy-content="{
    &quot;samplers&quot;: [
        {
            &quot;magFilter&quot;: 9729,
            &quot;minFilter&quot;: 9987,
            &quot;wrapS&quot;: 10497,
            &quot;wrapT&quot;: 10497
        }
    ]
}">

    {
        "samplers": [
            {
                "magFilter": 9729,
                "minFilter": 9987,
                "wrapS": 10497,
                "wrapT": 10497
            }
        ]
    }

</div>

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

##### 3.8.4.5. Non-power-of-two Textures

<a href="#3845-non-power-of-two-textures"
id="user-content-3845-non-power-of-two-textures" class="anchor"
aria-label="Permalink: 3.8.4.5. Non-power-of-two Textures"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Client implementations **SHOULD** resize non-power-of-two textures (so
that their horizontal and vertical sizes are powers of two) when running
on platforms that have limited support for such texture dimensions.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 50%" />
<col style="width: 50%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><div dir="auto">
Note
</div></td>
<td><div dir="auto">
Implementation Note
</div>
<div dir="auto">
<p>Specifically, if the <code>sampler</code> the texture references:</p>
</div>
<div dir="auto">
<ul>
<li><p>has a wrapping mode (either <code>wrapS</code> or
<code>wrapT</code>) equal to <em>repeat</em> or <em>mirrored
repeat</em>, or</p></li>
<li><p>has a minification filter (<code>minFilter</code>) that uses
mipmapping.</p></li>
</ul>
</div></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

</div>

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

### 3.9. Materials

<a href="#39-materials" id="user-content-39-materials" class="anchor"
aria-label="Permalink: 3.9. Materials"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

#### 3.9.1. Overview

<a href="#391-overview" id="user-content-391-overview" class="anchor"
aria-label="Permalink: 3.9.1. Overview"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

glTF defines materials using a common set of parameters that are based
on widely used material representations from Physically Based Rendering
(PBR). Specifically, glTF uses the metallic-roughness material model.
Using this declarative representation of materials enables a glTF file
to be rendered consistently across platforms.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div dir="auto">

<a
href="/KhronosGroup/glTF/blob/main/specification/2.0/figures/materials.svg"
target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer"><img
src="/KhronosGroup/glTF/raw/main/specification/2.0/figures/materials.svg"
style="max-width: 100%;" alt="materials" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Figure 7. Physically Based Rendering Example

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

#### 3.9.2. Metallic-Roughness Material

<a href="#392-metallic-roughness-material"
id="user-content-392-metallic-roughness-material" class="anchor"
aria-label="Permalink: 3.9.2. Metallic-Roughness Material"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

All parameters related to the metallic-roughness material model are
defined under the `pbrMetallicRoughness` property of `material` object.
The following example shows how to define a gold-like material using the
metallic-roughness parameters:

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div dir="auto">

<div class="highlight highlight-source-json notranslate position-relative overflow-auto"
dir="auto" snippet-clipboard-copy-content="{
    &quot;materials&quot;: [
        {
            &quot;name&quot;: &quot;gold&quot;,
            &quot;pbrMetallicRoughness&quot;: {
                &quot;baseColorFactor&quot;: [ 1.000, 0.766, 0.336, 1.0 ],
                &quot;metallicFactor&quot;: 1.0,
                &quot;roughnessFactor&quot;: 0.0
            }
        }
    ]
}">

    {
        "materials": [
            {
                "name": "gold",
                "pbrMetallicRoughness": {
                    "baseColorFactor": [ 1.000, 0.766, 0.336, 1.0 ],
                    "metallicFactor": 1.0,
                    "roughnessFactor": 0.0
                }
            }
        ]
    }

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

The metallic-roughness material model is defined by the following
properties:

</div>

<div dir="auto">

- *base color* - The base color of the material.

- *metalness* - The metalness of the material; values range from `0.0`
  (non-metal) to `1.0` (metal); see [Appendix
  B](#appendix-b-brdf-implementation) for the interpretation of
  intermediate values.

- *roughness* - The roughness of the material; values range from `0.0`
  (smooth) to `1.0` (rough).

</div>

<div dir="auto">

The *base color* has two different interpretations depending on the
value of *metalness*. When the material is a metal, the base color is
the specific measured reflectance value at normal incidence (F0). For a
non-metal the base color represents the reflected diffuse color of the
material. In this model it is not possible to specify a F0 value for
non-metals, and a linear value of 4% (0.04) is used.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

The value for each property **MAY** be defined using factors and/or
textures (e.g., `baseColorTexture` and `baseColorFactor`). If a texture
is not given, all respective texture components within this material
model **MUST** be assumed to have a value of `1.0`. If both factors and
textures are present, the factor value acts as a linear multiplier for
the corresponding texture values. A texture binding is defined by an
`index` of a *texture* object and an optional index of texture
coordinates.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

The following example shows a material that uses a texture for its *base
color* property.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div dir="auto">

<div class="highlight highlight-source-json notranslate position-relative overflow-auto"
dir="auto" snippet-clipboard-copy-content="{
    &quot;materials&quot;: [
        {
            &quot;pbrMetallicRoughness&quot;: {
                &quot;baseColorTexture&quot;: {
                    &quot;index&quot;: 0,
                    &quot;texCoord&quot;: 1
                },
            }
        }
    ],
    &quot;textures&quot;: [
        {
            &quot;source&quot;: 0
        }
    ],
    &quot;images&quot;: [
        {
            &quot;uri&quot;: &quot;base_color.png&quot;
        }
    ]
}">

    {
        "materials": [
            {
                "pbrMetallicRoughness": {
                    "baseColorTexture": {
                        "index": 0,
                        "texCoord": 1
                    },
                }
            }
        ],
        "textures": [
            {
                "source": 0
            }
        ],
        "images": [
            {
                "uri": "base_color.png"
            }
        ]
    }

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

The *base color* texture **MUST** contain 8-bit values encoded with the
[sRGB opto-electronic transfer function](#srgb) so RGB values **MUST**
be decoded to real linear values before they are used for any
computations. To achieve correct filtering, the transfer function
**SHOULD** be decoded before performing linear interpolation.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

The textures for *metalness* and *roughness* properties are packed
together in a single texture called `metallicRoughnessTexture`. Its
*green* channel contains roughness values and its *blue* channel
contains metalness values. This texture **MUST** be encoded with linear
transfer function and **MAY** use more than 8 bits per channel.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

For example, assume an 8-bit RGBA value of `[64, 124, 231, 255]` is
sampled from `baseColorTexture` and assume that `baseColorFactor` is
given as `[0.2, 1.0, 0.7, 1.0]`. Then, the final *base color* value
would be (after decoding the transfer function and multiplying by the
factor)

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div dir="auto">

<div class="highlight highlight-source-c notranslate position-relative overflow-auto"
dir="auto"
snippet-clipboard-copy-content="[0.051 * 0.2, 0.202 * 1.0, 0.799 * 0.7, 1.0 * 1.0] = [0.0102, 0.202, 0.5593, 1.0]">

    [0.051 * 0.2, 0.202 * 1.0, 0.799 * 0.7, 1.0 * 1.0] = [0.0102, 0.202, 0.5593, 1.0]

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

In addition to the material properties, if a primitive specifies a
vertex color using the attribute semantic property `COLOR_0`, then this
value acts as an additional linear multiplier to *base color*.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Implementations of the bidirectional reflectance distribution function
(BRDF) itself **MAY** vary based on device performance and resource
constraints. See [Appendix B](#appendix-b-brdf-implementation) for more
details on the BRDF calculations.

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

#### 3.9.3. Additional Textures

<a href="#393-additional-textures"
id="user-content-393-additional-textures" class="anchor"
aria-label="Permalink: 3.9.3. Additional Textures"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

The material definition also provides for additional textures that
**MAY** also be used with the metallic-roughness material model as well
as other material models, which could be provided via glTF extensions.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

The following additional textures are supported:

</div>

<div dir="auto">

- **normal** : A tangent space normal texture. The texture encodes XYZ
  components of a normal vector in tangent space as RGB values stored
  with linear transfer function. Normal textures **SHOULD NOT** contain
  *alpha* channel as it not used anyway. After dequantization, texel
  values **MUST** be mapped as follows: *red* \[0.0 .. 1.0\] to X \[-1
  .. 1\], *green* \[0.0 .. 1.0\] to Y \[-1 .. 1\], *blue* (0.5 .. 1.0\]
  maps to Z (0 .. 1\]. Normal textures **SHOULD NOT** contain blue
  values less than or equal to `0.5`.

  <div dir="auto">

  <table>
  <colgroup>
  <col style="width: 50%" />
  <col style="width: 50%" />
  </colgroup>
  <tbody>
  <tr>
  <td><div dir="auto">
  Note
  </div></td>
  <td><div dir="auto">
  Implementation Note
  </div>
  <div dir="auto">
  <p>This mapping is usually implemented as
  <code>sampledValue * 2.0 - 1.0</code>.</p>
  </div></td>
  </tr>
  </tbody>
  </table>

  </div>

  <div dir="auto">

  The texture binding for normal textures **MAY** additionally contain a
  scalar `scale` value that linearly scales X and Y components of the
  normal vector.

  </div>

  <div dir="auto">

  Normal vectors **MUST** be normalized before being used in lighting
  equations. When scaling is used, vector normalization happens after
  scaling.

  </div>

- **occlusion** : The occlusion texture; it indicates areas that receive
  less indirect lighting from ambient sources. Direct lighting is not
  affected. The *red* channel of the texture encodes the occlusion
  value, where `0.0` means fully-occluded area (no indirect lighting)
  and `1.0` means not occluded area (full indirect lighting). Other
  texture channels (if present) do not affect occlusion.

  <div dir="auto">

  The texture binding for occlusion maps **MAY** optionally contain a
  scalar `strength` value that is used to reduce the occlusion effect.
  When present, it affects the occlusion value as
  `1.0 + strength * (occlusionTexture - 1.0)`.

  </div>

- **emissive** : The emissive texture and factor control the color and
  intensity of the light being emitted by the material. The texture
  **MUST** contain 8-bit values encoded with the [sRGB opto-electronic
  transfer function](#srgb) so RGB values **MUST** be decoded to real
  linear values before they are used for any computations. To achieve
  correct filtering, the transfer function **SHOULD** be decoded before
  performing linear interpolation.

  <div dir="auto">

  For implementations where a physical light unit is needed, the units
  for the multiplicative product of the emissive texture and factor are
  candela per square meter (**cd / m<sup>2</sup>**), sometimes called
  *nits*.

  </div>

  <div dir="auto">

  <table>
  <colgroup>
  <col style="width: 50%" />
  <col style="width: 50%" />
  </colgroup>
  <tbody>
  <tr>
  <td><div dir="auto">
  Note
  </div></td>
  <td><div dir="auto">
  Implementation Note
  </div>
  <div dir="auto">
  <p>Because the value is specified per square meter, it indicates the
  brightness of any given point along the surface. However, the exact
  conversion from physical light units to the brightness of rendered
  pixels requires knowledge of the camera’s exposure settings, which are
  left as an implementation detail unless otherwise defined by a glTF
  extension.</p>
  </div>
  <div dir="auto">
  <p>Many rendering engines simplify this calculation by assuming that an
  emissive factor of <code>1.0</code> results in a fully exposed
  pixel.</p>
  </div></td>
  </tr>
  </tbody>
  </table>

  </div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

The following example shows a material that is defined using
`pbrMetallicRoughness` parameters as well as additional textures:

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div dir="auto">

<div class="highlight highlight-source-json notranslate position-relative overflow-auto"
dir="auto" snippet-clipboard-copy-content="{
    &quot;materials&quot;: [
        {
            &quot;name&quot;: &quot;Material0&quot;,
            &quot;pbrMetallicRoughness&quot;: {
                &quot;baseColorFactor&quot;: [ 0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 1.0 ],
                &quot;baseColorTexture&quot;: {
                    &quot;index&quot;: 1,
                    &quot;texCoord&quot;: 1
                },
                &quot;metallicFactor&quot;: 1,
                &quot;roughnessFactor&quot;: 1,
                &quot;metallicRoughnessTexture&quot;: {
                    &quot;index&quot;: 2,
                    &quot;texCoord&quot;: 1
                }
            },
            &quot;normalTexture&quot;: {
                &quot;scale&quot;: 2,
                &quot;index&quot;: 3,
                &quot;texCoord&quot;: 1
            },
            &quot;emissiveFactor&quot;: [ 0.2, 0.1, 0.0 ]
        }
    ]
}">

    {
        "materials": [
            {
                "name": "Material0",
                "pbrMetallicRoughness": {
                    "baseColorFactor": [ 0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 1.0 ],
                    "baseColorTexture": {
                        "index": 1,
                        "texCoord": 1
                    },
                    "metallicFactor": 1,
                    "roughnessFactor": 1,
                    "metallicRoughnessTexture": {
                        "index": 2,
                        "texCoord": 1
                    }
                },
                "normalTexture": {
                    "scale": 2,
                    "index": 3,
                    "texCoord": 1
                },
                "emissiveFactor": [ 0.2, 0.1, 0.0 ]
            }
        ]
    }

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

If a client implementation is resource-bound and cannot support all the
textures defined it **SHOULD** support these additional textures in the
following priority order. Resource-bound implementations **SHOULD** drop
textures from the bottom to the top.

</div>

| Texture | Rendering impact when feature is not supported |
|----|----|
| Normal | Geometry will appear less detailed than authored. |
| Occlusion | Model will appear brighter in areas that are intended to be darker. |
| Emissive | Model with lights will not be lit. For example, the headlights of a car model will be off instead of on. |

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

#### 3.9.4. Alpha Coverage

<a href="#394-alpha-coverage" id="user-content-394-alpha-coverage"
class="anchor" aria-label="Permalink: 3.9.4. Alpha Coverage"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

The `alphaMode` property defines how the alpha value is interpreted. The
alpha value is taken from the fourth component of the *base color* for
metallic-roughness material model.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

`alphaMode` can be one of the following values:

</div>

<div dir="auto">

- `OPAQUE` - The rendered output is fully opaque and any alpha value is
  ignored.

- `MASK` - The rendered output is either fully opaque or fully
  transparent depending on the alpha value and the specified *alpha
  cutoff* value; the exact appearance of the edges **MAY** be subject to
  implementation-specific techniques such as “Alpha-to-Coverage”.

  <div dir="auto">

  <table>
  <colgroup>
  <col style="width: 50%" />
  <col style="width: 50%" />
  </colgroup>
  <tbody>
  <tr>
  <td><div dir="auto">
  Note
  </div></td>
  <td><div dir="auto">
  Note
  </div>
  <div dir="auto">
  <p>This mode is used to simulate geometry such as tree leaves or wire
  fences.</p>
  </div></td>
  </tr>
  </tbody>
  </table>

  </div>

- `BLEND` - The rendered output is combined with the background using
  the “over” operator as described in [Compositing digital
  images](#compositing).

  <div dir="auto">

  <table>
  <colgroup>
  <col style="width: 50%" />
  <col style="width: 50%" />
  </colgroup>
  <tbody>
  <tr>
  <td><div dir="auto">
  Note
  </div></td>
  <td><div dir="auto">
  Note
  </div>
  <div dir="auto">
  <p>This mode is used to simulate geometry such as gauze cloth or animal
  fur.</p>
  </div></td>
  </tr>
  </tbody>
  </table>

  </div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

When `alphaMode` is set to `MASK` the `alphaCutoff` property specifies
the cutoff threshold. If the alpha value is greater than or equal to the
`alphaCutoff` value then it is rendered as fully opaque, otherwise, it
is rendered as fully transparent. `alphaCutoff` value is ignored for
other modes.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 50%" />
<col style="width: 50%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><div dir="auto">
Note
</div></td>
<td><div dir="auto">
Implementation Note for Real-Time Rasterizers
</div>
<div dir="auto">
<p>Real-time rasterizers typically use depth buffers and mesh sorting to
support alpha modes. The following describe the expected behavior for
these types of renderers.</p>
</div>
<div dir="auto">
<ul>
<li><p><code>OPAQUE</code> - A depth value is written for every pixel
and mesh sorting is not required for correct output.</p></li>
<li><p><code>MASK</code> - A depth value is not written for a pixel that
is discarded after the alpha test. A depth value is written for all
other pixels. Mesh sorting is not required for correct output.</p></li>
<li><p><code>BLEND</code> - Support for this mode varies. There is no
perfect and fast solution that works for all cases. Client
implementations should try to achieve the correct blending output for as
many situations as possible. Whether depth value is written or whether
to sort is up to the implementation. For example, implementations may
discard pixels that have zero or close to zero alpha value to avoid
sorting issues.</p></li>
</ul>
</div></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

#### 3.9.5. Double Sided

<a href="#395-double-sided" id="user-content-395-double-sided"
class="anchor" aria-label="Permalink: 3.9.5. Double Sided"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

The `doubleSided` property specifies whether the material is double
sided.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

When this value is false, back-face culling is enabled, i.e., only
front-facing triangles are rendered.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

When this value is true, back-face culling is disabled and double sided
lighting is enabled. The back-face **MUST** have its normals reversed
before the lighting equation is evaluated.

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

#### 3.9.6. Default Material

<a href="#396-default-material" id="user-content-396-default-material"
class="anchor" aria-label="Permalink: 3.9.6. Default Material"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

The default material, used when a mesh does not specify a material, is
defined to be a material with no properties specified. All the default
values of [`material`](#reference-material) apply.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 50%" />
<col style="width: 50%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><div dir="auto">
Note
</div></td>
<td><div dir="auto">
Implementation Note
</div>
<div dir="auto">
<p>This material does not emit light and will be black unless some
lighting is present in the scene.</p>
</div></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

#### 3.9.7. Point and Line Materials

<a href="#397-point-and-line-materials"
id="user-content-397-point-and-line-materials" class="anchor"
aria-label="Permalink: 3.9.7. Point and Line Materials"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

This specification does not define size or style of non-triangular
primitives (such as *points* or *lines*), and applications **MAY** use
various techniques to render these primitives as appropriate. However,
the following conventions are **RECOMMENDED** for consistency:

</div>

<div dir="auto">

- Points and Lines **SHOULD** have widths of 1px in viewport space.

- Points or Lines with `NORMAL` and `TANGENT` attributes **SHOULD** be
  rendered with standard lighting including normal textures.

- Points or Lines with `NORMAL` but without `TANGENT` attributes
  **SHOULD** be rendered with standard lighting but ignoring any normal
  textures on the material.

- Points or Lines with no `NORMAL` attribute **SHOULD** be rendered
  without lighting and instead use the sum of the *base color* value (as
  defined above, multiplied by `COLOR_0` when present) and the
  *emissive* value.

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

### 3.10. Cameras

<a href="#310-cameras" id="user-content-310-cameras" class="anchor"
aria-label="Permalink: 3.10. Cameras"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

#### 3.10.1. Overview

<a href="#3101-overview" id="user-content-3101-overview" class="anchor"
aria-label="Permalink: 3.10.1. Overview"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Cameras are stored in the asset’s `cameras` array. Each camera defines a
`type` property that designates the type of projection (perspective or
orthographic), and either a `perspective` or `orthographic` property
that defines the details. A camera is instantiated within a node using
the `node.camera` property.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

A camera object defines the projection matrix that transforms scene
coordinates from the view space to the clip space.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

A node containing the camera instance defines the view matrix that
transforms scene coordinates from the global space to the view space.

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

#### 3.10.2. View Matrix

<a href="#3102-view-matrix" id="user-content-3102-view-matrix"
class="anchor" aria-label="Permalink: 3.10.2. View Matrix"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

The camera is defined such that the local +X axis is to the right, the
“lens” looks towards the local -Z axis, and the top of the camera is
aligned with the local +Y axis.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

The view matrix is derived from the global transform of the node
containing the camera with the scaling ignored. If the node’s global
transform is identity, the location of the camera is at the origin.

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

#### 3.10.3. Projection Matrices

<a href="#3103-projection-matrices"
id="user-content-3103-projection-matrices" class="anchor"
aria-label="Permalink: 3.10.3. Projection Matrices"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

##### 3.10.3.1. Overview

<a href="#31031-overview" id="user-content-31031-overview"
class="anchor" aria-label="Permalink: 3.10.3.1. Overview"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

The projection can be perspective or orthographic.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

There are two subtypes of perspective projections: finite and infinite.
When the `zfar` property is undefined, the camera defines an infinite
projection. Otherwise, the camera defines a finite projection.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

The following example defines two perspective cameras with supplied
values for Y field of view, aspect ratio, and clipping information.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div dir="auto">

<div class="highlight highlight-source-json notranslate position-relative overflow-auto"
dir="auto" snippet-clipboard-copy-content="{
    &quot;cameras&quot;: [
        {
            &quot;name&quot;: &quot;Finite perspective camera&quot;,
            &quot;type&quot;: &quot;perspective&quot;,
            &quot;perspective&quot;: {
                &quot;aspectRatio&quot;: 1.5,
                &quot;yfov&quot;: 0.660593,
                &quot;zfar&quot;: 100,
                &quot;znear&quot;: 0.01
            }
        },
        {
            &quot;name&quot;: &quot;Infinite perspective camera&quot;,
            &quot;type&quot;: &quot;perspective&quot;,
            &quot;perspective&quot;: {
                &quot;aspectRatio&quot;: 1.5,
                &quot;yfov&quot;: 0.660593,
                &quot;znear&quot;: 0.01
            }
        }
    ]
}">

    {
        "cameras": [
            {
                "name": "Finite perspective camera",
                "type": "perspective",
                "perspective": {
                    "aspectRatio": 1.5,
                    "yfov": 0.660593,
                    "zfar": 100,
                    "znear": 0.01
                }
            },
            {
                "name": "Infinite perspective camera",
                "type": "perspective",
                "perspective": {
                    "aspectRatio": 1.5,
                    "yfov": 0.660593,
                    "znear": 0.01
                }
            }
        ]
    }

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Client implementations **SHOULD** use the following projection matrices.

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

##### 3.10.3.2. Infinite perspective projection

<a href="#31032-infinite-perspective-projection"
id="user-content-31032-infinite-perspective-projection" class="anchor"
aria-label="Permalink: 3.10.3.2. Infinite perspective projection"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Let

</div>

<div dir="auto">

- `a` be the aspect ratio (width over height) of the field of view, set
  by `camera.perspective.aspectRatio`, or the aspect ratio of the
  viewport;

- `y` be the vertical field of view in radians, set by
  `camera.perspective.yfov`;

- `n` be the distance to the near clipping plane, set by
  `camera.perspective.znear`.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Then, the projection matrix is defined as follows.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 50%" />
<col style="width: 50%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><div dir="auto">
Note
</div></td>
<td><div dir="auto">
Note
</div>
<div dir="auto">
<p>This section contains formulas that may not display correctly in all
preview tools. View the full <a
href="https://www.khronos.org/registry/glTF/specs/2.0/glTF-2.0.html#infinite-perspective-projection"
rel="nofollow">infinite perspective projection</a>.</p>
</div></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div dir="auto">

\\\begin{bmatrix} 1 \over { a \times \tan(0.5 \times y) } & 0 & 0 & 0 \\
0 & 1 \over { \tan(0.5 \times y) } & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 & -2n \\ 0 & 0
& -1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\\

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

When the provided camera’s aspect ratio does not match the aspect ratio
of the viewport, client implementations **SHOULD NOT** crop or perform
non-uniform scaling (“stretching”) to fill the viewport.

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

##### 3.10.3.3. Finite perspective projection

<a href="#31033-finite-perspective-projection"
id="user-content-31033-finite-perspective-projection" class="anchor"
aria-label="Permalink: 3.10.3.3. Finite perspective projection"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Let

</div>

<div dir="auto">

- `a` be the aspect ratio (width over height) of the field of view, set
  by `camera.perspective.aspectRatio`, or the aspect ratio of the
  viewport;

- `y` be the vertical field of view in radians, set by
  `camera.perspective.yfov`;

- `f` be the distance to the far clipping plane, set by
  `camera.perspective.zfar`;

- `n` be the distance to the near clipping plane, set by
  `camera.perspective.znear`.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Then, the projection matrix is defined as follows.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 50%" />
<col style="width: 50%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><div dir="auto">
Note
</div></td>
<td><div dir="auto">
Note
</div>
<div dir="auto">
<p>This section contains formulas that may not display correctly in all
preview tools. View the full <a
href="https://www.khronos.org/registry/glTF/specs/2.0/glTF-2.0.html#finite-perspective-projection"
rel="nofollow">finite perspective projection</a>.</p>
</div></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div dir="auto">

\\\begin{bmatrix} 1 \over { a \times \tan(0.5 \times y) } & 0 & 0 & 0 \\
0 & 1 \over { \tan(0.5 \times y) } & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & { f + n } \over {
n - f } & { 2 f n } \over { n - f } \\ 0 & 0 & -1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\\

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

When the provided camera’s aspect ratio does not match the aspect ratio
of the viewport, client implementations **SHOULD NOT** crop or perform
non-uniform scaling (“stretching”) to fill the viewport.

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

##### 3.10.3.4. Orthographic projection

<a href="#31034-orthographic-projection"
id="user-content-31034-orthographic-projection" class="anchor"
aria-label="Permalink: 3.10.3.4. Orthographic projection"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Let

</div>

<div dir="auto">

- `r` be half the orthographic width, set by `camera.orthographic.xmag`;

- `t` be half the orthographic height, set by
  `camera.orthographic.ymag`;

- `f` be the distance to the far clipping plane, set by
  `camera.orthographic.zfar`;

- `n` be the distance to the near clipping plane, set by
  `camera.orthographic.znear`.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Then, the projection matrix is defined as follows.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 50%" />
<col style="width: 50%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><div dir="auto">
Note
</div></td>
<td><div dir="auto">
Note
</div>
<div dir="auto">
<p>This section contains formulas that may not display correctly in all
preview tools. View the full <a
href="https://www.khronos.org/registry/glTF/specs/2.0/glTF-2.0.html#orthographic-projection"
rel="nofollow">orthographic projection</a>.</p>
</div></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div dir="auto">

\\\begin{bmatrix} 1 \over r & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \over t & 0 & 0 \\ 0 &
0 & 2 \over { n - f } & { f + n } \over { n - f } \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1
\end{bmatrix}\\

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

When `r / t` does not match the aspect ratio of the viewport, client
implementations **SHOULD NOT** crop or perform non-uniform scaling
(“stretching”) to fill the viewport.

</div>

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

### 3.11. Animations

<a href="#311-animations" id="user-content-311-animations"
class="anchor" aria-label="Permalink: 3.11. Animations"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

glTF supports articulated and skinned animation via key frame animations
of nodes' transforms. Key frame data is stored in buffers and referenced
in animations using accessors.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

glTF 2.0 also supports animation of instantiated morph targets in a
similar fashion.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 50%" />
<col style="width: 50%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><div dir="auto">
Note
</div></td>
<td><div dir="auto">
Note
</div>
<div dir="auto">
<p>glTF 2.0 only supports animating node transforms and morph target
weights. Extensions or a future version of the specification may support
animating arbitrary properties, such as material colors and texture
transformation matrices.</p>
</div></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 50%" />
<col style="width: 50%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><div dir="auto">
Note
</div></td>
<td><div dir="auto">
Note
</div>
<div dir="auto">
<p>glTF 2.0 defines only storage of animation keyframes, so this
specification doesn’t define any runtime behavior, such as: order of
playing, auto-start, loops, mapping of timelines, etc. When loading a
glTF 2.0 asset, client implementations may select an animation entry and
pause it on the first frame, play it automatically, or ignore all
animations until further user requests. When a playing animation is
stopped, client implementations may reset the scene to the initial state
or freeze it at the current frame.</p>
</div></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 50%" />
<col style="width: 50%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><div dir="auto">
Note
</div></td>
<td><div dir="auto">
Implementation Note
</div>
<div dir="auto">
<p>glTF 2.0 does not specifically define how an animation will be used
when imported but, as a best practice, it is recommended that each
animation is self-contained as an action. For example, “Walk” and “Run”
animations might each contain multiple channels targeting a model’s
various bones. The client implementation may choose when to play any of
the available animations.</p>
</div></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

All animations are stored in the `animations` array of the asset. An
animation is defined as a set of channels (the `channels` property) and
a set of samplers that specify accessors with key frame data and
interpolation method (the `samplers` property).

</div>

<div dir="auto">

The following examples show the expected usage of animations.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div dir="auto">

<div class="highlight highlight-source-json notranslate position-relative overflow-auto"
dir="auto" snippet-clipboard-copy-content="{
    &quot;animations&quot;: [
        {
            &quot;name&quot;: &quot;Animate all properties of one node with different samplers&quot;,
            &quot;channels&quot;: [
                {
                    &quot;sampler&quot;: 0,
                    &quot;target&quot;: {
                        &quot;node&quot;: 1,
                        &quot;path&quot;: &quot;rotation&quot;
                    }
                },
                {
                    &quot;sampler&quot;: 1,
                    &quot;target&quot;: {
                        &quot;node&quot;: 1,
                        &quot;path&quot;: &quot;scale&quot;
                    }
                },
                {
                    &quot;sampler&quot;: 2,
                    &quot;target&quot;: {
