                        &quot;node&quot;: 1,
                        &quot;path&quot;: &quot;translation&quot;
                    }
                }
            ],
            &quot;samplers&quot;: [
                {
                    &quot;input&quot;: 4,
                    &quot;interpolation&quot;: &quot;LINEAR&quot;,
                    &quot;output&quot;: 5
                },
                {
                    &quot;input&quot;: 4,
                    &quot;interpolation&quot;: &quot;LINEAR&quot;,
                    &quot;output&quot;: 6
                },
                {
                    &quot;input&quot;: 4,
                    &quot;interpolation&quot;: &quot;LINEAR&quot;,
                    &quot;output&quot;: 7
                }
            ]
        },
        {
            &quot;name&quot;: &quot;Animate two nodes with different samplers&quot;,
            &quot;channels&quot;: [
                {
                    &quot;sampler&quot;: 0,
                    &quot;target&quot;: {
                        &quot;node&quot;: 0,
                        &quot;path&quot;: &quot;rotation&quot;
                    }
                },
                {
                    &quot;sampler&quot;: 1,
                    &quot;target&quot;: {
                        &quot;node&quot;: 1,
                        &quot;path&quot;: &quot;rotation&quot;
                    }
                }
            ],
            &quot;samplers&quot;: [
                {
                    &quot;input&quot;: 0,
                    &quot;interpolation&quot;: &quot;LINEAR&quot;,
                    &quot;output&quot;: 1
                },
                {
                    &quot;input&quot;: 2,
                    &quot;interpolation&quot;: &quot;LINEAR&quot;,
                    &quot;output&quot;: 3
                }
            ]
        },
        {
            &quot;name&quot;: &quot;Animate two nodes with the same sampler&quot;,
            &quot;channels&quot;: [
                {
                    &quot;sampler&quot;: 0,
                    &quot;target&quot;: {
                        &quot;node&quot;: 0,
                        &quot;path&quot;: &quot;rotation&quot;
                    }
                },
                {
                    &quot;sampler&quot;: 0,
                    &quot;target&quot;: {
                        &quot;node&quot;: 1,
                        &quot;path&quot;: &quot;rotation&quot;
                    }
                }
            ],
            &quot;samplers&quot;: [
                {
                    &quot;input&quot;: 0,
                    &quot;interpolation&quot;: &quot;LINEAR&quot;,
                    &quot;output&quot;: 1
                }
            ]
        },
        {
            &quot;name&quot;: &quot;Animate a node rotation channel and the weights of a Morph Target it instantiates&quot;,
            &quot;channels&quot;: [
                {
                    &quot;sampler&quot;: 0,
                    &quot;target&quot;: {
                        &quot;node&quot;: 1,
                        &quot;path&quot;: &quot;rotation&quot;
                    }
                },
                {
                    &quot;sampler&quot;: 1,
                    &quot;target&quot;: {
                        &quot;node&quot;: 1,
                        &quot;path&quot;: &quot;weights&quot;
                    }
                }
            ],
            &quot;samplers&quot;: [
                {
                    &quot;input&quot;: 4,
                    &quot;interpolation&quot;: &quot;LINEAR&quot;,
                    &quot;output&quot;: 5
                },
                {
                    &quot;input&quot;: 4,
                    &quot;interpolation&quot;: &quot;LINEAR&quot;,
                    &quot;output&quot;: 6
                }
            ]
        }
    ]
}">

    {
        "animations": [
            {
                "name": "Animate all properties of one node with different samplers",
                "channels": [
                    {
                        "sampler": 0,
                        "target": {
                            "node": 1,
                            "path": "rotation"
                        }
                    },
                    {
                        "sampler": 1,
                        "target": {
                            "node": 1,
                            "path": "scale"
                        }
                    },
                    {
                        "sampler": 2,
                        "target": {
                            "node": 1,
                            "path": "translation"
                        }
                    }
                ],
                "samplers": [
                    {
                        "input": 4,
                        "interpolation": "LINEAR",
                        "output": 5
                    },
                    {
                        "input": 4,
                        "interpolation": "LINEAR",
                        "output": 6
                    },
                    {
                        "input": 4,
                        "interpolation": "LINEAR",
                        "output": 7
                    }
                ]
            },
            {
                "name": "Animate two nodes with different samplers",
                "channels": [
                    {
                        "sampler": 0,
                        "target": {
                            "node": 0,
                            "path": "rotation"
                        }
                    },
                    {
                        "sampler": 1,
                        "target": {
                            "node": 1,
                            "path": "rotation"
                        }
                    }
                ],
                "samplers": [
                    {
                        "input": 0,
                        "interpolation": "LINEAR",
                        "output": 1
                    },
                    {
                        "input": 2,
                        "interpolation": "LINEAR",
                        "output": 3
                    }
                ]
            },
            {
                "name": "Animate two nodes with the same sampler",
                "channels": [
                    {
                        "sampler": 0,
                        "target": {
                            "node": 0,
                            "path": "rotation"
                        }
                    },
                    {
                        "sampler": 0,
                        "target": {
                            "node": 1,
                            "path": "rotation"
                        }
                    }
                ],
                "samplers": [
                    {
                        "input": 0,
                        "interpolation": "LINEAR",
                        "output": 1
                    }
                ]
            },
            {
                "name": "Animate a node rotation channel and the weights of a Morph Target it instantiates",
                "channels": [
                    {
                        "sampler": 0,
                        "target": {
                            "node": 1,
                            "path": "rotation"
                        }
                    },
                    {
                        "sampler": 1,
                        "target": {
                            "node": 1,
                            "path": "weights"
                        }
                    }
                ],
                "samplers": [
                    {
                        "input": 4,
                        "interpolation": "LINEAR",
                        "output": 5
                    },
                    {
                        "input": 4,
                        "interpolation": "LINEAR",
                        "output": 6
                    }
                ]
            }
        ]
    }

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

*Channels* connect the output values of the key frame animation to a
specific node in the hierarchy. A channel’s `sampler` property contains
the index of one of the samplers present in the containing animation’s
`samplers` array. The `target` property is an object that identifies
which node to animate using its `node` property, and which property of
the node to animate using `path`. Non-animated properties **MUST** keep
their values during animation.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

When `node` isn’t defined, channel **SHOULD** be ignored. Valid path
names are `"translation"`, `"rotation"`, `"scale"`, and `"weights"`.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Nodes that do not contain a mesh with morph targets **MUST NOT** be
targeted with `"weights"` path.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Within one animation, each target (a combination of a node and a path)
**MUST NOT** be used more than once.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 50%" />
<col style="width: 50%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><div dir="auto">
Note
</div></td>
<td><div dir="auto">
Implementation Note
</div>
<div dir="auto">
<p>This prevents potential ambiguities when one target is affected by
two or more overlapping samplers.</p>
</div></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Each of the animation’s **samplers** defines the `input`/`output` pair:
a set of floating-point scalar values representing linear time in
seconds; and a set of vectors or scalars representing the animated
property. All values are stored in a buffer and accessed via accessors;
refer to the table below for output accessor types. Interpolation
between keys is performed using the interpolation method specified in
the `interpolation` property. Supported `interpolation` values include
`LINEAR`, `STEP`, and `CUBICSPLINE`. See [Appendix
C](#appendix-c-interpolation) for additional information about
interpolation modes.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

The inputs of each sampler are relative to `t = 0`, defined as the
beginning of the parent `animations` entry. Before and after the
provided input range, output **MUST** be clamped to the nearest end of
the input range.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 50%" />
<col style="width: 50%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><div dir="auto">
Note
</div></td>
<td><div dir="auto">
Implementation Note
</div>
<div dir="auto">
<p>For example, if the earliest sampler input for an animation is
<code>t = 10</code>, a client implementation must begin playback of that
animation channel at <code>t = 0</code> with output clamped to the first
available output value.</p>
</div></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Samplers within a given animation **MAY** have different inputs.

</div>

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 25%" />
<col style="width: 25%" />
<col style="width: 25%" />
<col style="width: 25%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th><code>channel.path</code></th>
<th>Accessor Type</th>
<th>Component Type(s)</th>
<th>Description</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><p><code>"translation"</code></p></td>
<td><p><code>"VEC3"</code></p></td>
<td><p><em>float</em></p></td>
<td><p>XYZ translation vector</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><p><code>"rotation"</code></p></td>
<td><p><code>"VEC4"</code></p></td>
<td><p><em>float</em><br />
<em>signed byte</em> normalized<br />
<em>unsigned byte</em> normalized<br />
<em>signed short</em> normalized<br />
<em>unsigned short</em> normalized</p></td>
<td><p>XYZW rotation quaternion</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><p><code>"scale"</code></p></td>
<td><p><code>"VEC3"</code></p></td>
<td><p><em>float</em></p></td>
<td><p>XYZ scale vector</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><p><code>"weights"</code></p></td>
<td><p><code>"SCALAR"</code></p></td>
<td><p><em>float</em><br />
<em>signed byte</em> normalized<br />
<em>unsigned byte</em> normalized<br />
<em>signed short</em> normalized<br />
<em>unsigned short</em> normalized</p></td>
<td><p>Weights of morph targets</p></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

<div dir="auto">

Implementations **MUST** use following equations to decode real
floating-point value `f` from a normalized integer `c` and vise-versa:

</div>

| `accessor.componentType` | int-to-float | float-to-int |
|----|----|----|
| *signed byte* | `f = max(c / 127.0, -1.0)` | `c = round(f * 127.0)` |
| *unsigned byte* | `f = c / 255.0` | `c = round(f * 255.0)` |
| *signed short* | `f = max(c / 32767.0, -1.0)` | `c = round(f * 32767.0)` |
| *unsigned short* | `f = c / 65535.0` | `c = round(f * 65535.0)` |

<div dir="auto">

Animation sampler’s `input` accessor **MUST** have its `min` and `max`
properties defined.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 50%" />
<col style="width: 50%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><div dir="auto">
Note
</div></td>
<td><div dir="auto">
Implementation Note
</div>
<div dir="auto">
<p>Animations with non-linear time inputs, such as time warps in
Autodesk 3ds Max or Maya, are not directly representable with glTF
animations. glTF is a runtime format and non-linear time inputs are
expensive to compute at runtime. Exporter implementations should sample
a non-linear time animation into linear inputs and outputs for an
accurate representation.</p>
</div></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

A morph target animation frame is defined by a sequence of scalars of
length equal to the number of targets in the animated morph target.
These scalar sequences **MUST** lie end-to-end as a single stream in the
output accessor, whose final size is equal to the number of morph
targets times the number of animation frames.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Morph target animation is by nature sparse, consider using [Sparse
Accessors](#sparse-accessors) for storage of morph target animation.
When used with `CUBICSPLINE` interpolation, tangents (a<sub>k</sub>,
b<sub>k</sub>) and values (v<sub>k</sub>) are grouped within keyframes:

</div>

<div dir="auto">

a<sub>1</sub>,a<sub>2</sub>,…​a<sub>n</sub>,v<sub>1</sub>,v<sub>2</sub>,…​v<sub>n</sub>,b<sub>1</sub>,b<sub>2</sub>,…​b<sub>n</sub>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

See [Appendix C](#appendix-c-interpolation) for additional information
about interpolation modes.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Skinned animation is achieved by animating the joints in the skin’s
joint hierarchy.

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

### 3.12. Specifying Extensions

<a href="#312-specifying-extensions"
id="user-content-312-specifying-extensions" class="anchor"
aria-label="Permalink: 3.12. Specifying Extensions"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

glTF defines an extension mechanism that allows the base format to be
extended with new capabilities. Any glTF object **MAY** have an optional
`extensions` property, as in the following example:

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div dir="auto">

<div class="highlight highlight-source-json notranslate position-relative overflow-auto"
dir="auto" snippet-clipboard-copy-content="{
    &quot;material&quot;: [
        {
            &quot;extensions&quot;: {
                &quot;KHR_materials_sheen&quot;: {
                    &quot;sheenColorFactor&quot;: [
                        1.0,
                        0.329,
                        0.1
                    ],
                    &quot;sheenRoughnessFactor&quot;: 0.8
                }
            }
        }
    ]
}">

    {
        "material": [
            {
                "extensions": {
                    "KHR_materials_sheen": {
                        "sheenColorFactor": [
                            1.0,
                            0.329,
                            0.1
                        ],
                        "sheenRoughnessFactor": 0.8
                    }
                }
            }
        ]
    }

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

All extensions used in a glTF asset **MUST** be listed in the top-level
`extensionsUsed` array object, e.g.,

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div dir="auto">

<div class="highlight highlight-source-json notranslate position-relative overflow-auto"
dir="auto" snippet-clipboard-copy-content="{
    &quot;extensionsUsed&quot;: [
        &quot;KHR_materials_sheen&quot;,
        &quot;VENDOR_physics&quot;
    ]
}">

    {
        "extensionsUsed": [
            "KHR_materials_sheen",
            "VENDOR_physics"
        ]
    }

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

All glTF extensions required to load and/or render an asset **MUST** be
listed in the top-level `extensionsRequired` array, e.g.,

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div dir="auto">

<div class="highlight highlight-source-json notranslate position-relative overflow-auto"
dir="auto" snippet-clipboard-copy-content="{
    &quot;extensionsRequired&quot;: [
        &quot;KHR_texture_transform&quot;
    ],
    &quot;extensionsUsed&quot;: [
        &quot;KHR_texture_transform&quot;
    ]
}">

    {
        "extensionsRequired": [
            "KHR_texture_transform"
        ],
        "extensionsUsed": [
            "KHR_texture_transform"
        ]
    }

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

`extensionsRequired` is a subset of `extensionsUsed`. All values in
`extensionsRequired` **MUST** also exist in `extensionsUsed`.

</div>

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

## 4. GLB File Format Specification

<a href="#4-glb-file-format-specification"
id="user-content-4-glb-file-format-specification" class="anchor"
aria-label="Permalink: 4. GLB File Format Specification"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

### 4.1. General (Informative)

<a href="#41-general-informative"
id="user-content-41-general-informative" class="anchor"
aria-label="Permalink: 4.1. General (Informative)"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

glTF provides two delivery options that can be used together:

</div>

<div dir="auto">

- glTF JSON points to external binary data (geometry, key frames,
  skins), and images.

- glTF JSON embeds base64-encoded binary data, and images inline using
  data URIs.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Hence, loading glTF files usually requires either separate requests to
fetch all binary data, or extra space due to base64-encoding.
Base64-encoding requires extra processing to decode and increases the
file size (by ~33% for encoded resources). While transport-layer gzip
mitigates the file size increase, decompression and decoding still add
significant loading time.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

To avoid this file size and processing overhead, a container format,
*Binary glTF* is introduced that enables a glTF asset, including JSON,
buffers, and images, to be stored in a single binary blob.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

A Binary glTF asset can still refer to external resources. For example,
an application that wants to keep images as separate files may embed
everything needed for a scene, except images, in a Binary glTF.

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

### 4.2. Structure

<a href="#42-structure" id="user-content-42-structure" class="anchor"
aria-label="Permalink: 4.2. Structure"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

A Binary glTF (which can be a file, for example) has the following
structure:

</div>

<div dir="auto">

- A 12-byte preamble, called the *header*.

- One or more *chunks* that contain JSON content and binary data.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

The *chunk* containing JSON **MAY** refer to external resources as
usual, and **MAY** also reference resources stored within other
*chunks*.

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

### 4.3. File Extension & Media Type

<a href="#43-file-extension--media-type"
id="user-content-43-file-extension--media-type" class="anchor"
aria-label="Permalink: 4.3. File Extension &amp; Media Type"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

The file extension to be used with Binary glTF is `.glb`.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

The registered media type is `model/gltf-binary`.

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

### 4.4. Binary glTF Layout

<a href="#44-binary-gltf-layout" id="user-content-44-binary-gltf-layout"
class="anchor" aria-label="Permalink: 4.4. Binary glTF Layout"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

#### 4.4.1. Overview

<a href="#441-overview" id="user-content-441-overview" class="anchor"
aria-label="Permalink: 4.4.1. Overview"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Binary glTF is little endian. The figure below shows an example of a
Binary glTF asset.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div dir="auto">

<a
href="/KhronosGroup/glTF/blob/main/specification/2.0/figures/glb2.svg"
target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer"><img
src="/KhronosGroup/glTF/raw/main/specification/2.0/figures/glb2.svg"
style="max-width: 100%;" alt="glb2" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Figure 8. Binary glTF Layout

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

The following sections describe the structure more in detail.

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

#### 4.4.2. Header

<a href="#442-header" id="user-content-442-header" class="anchor"
aria-label="Permalink: 4.4.2. Header"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

The 12-byte header consists of three 4-byte entries:

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div dir="auto">

<div class="highlight highlight-source-c notranslate position-relative overflow-auto"
dir="auto" snippet-clipboard-copy-content="uint32 magic
uint32 version
uint32 length">

    uint32 magic
    uint32 version
    uint32 length

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

- `magic` **MUST** be equal to equal `0x46546C67`. It is ASCII string
  `glTF` and can be used to identify data as Binary glTF.

- `version` indicates the version of the Binary glTF container format.
  This specification defines version 2.

  <div dir="auto">

  Client implementations that load GLB format **MUST** also check for
  the [asset version properties](#asset) in the JSON chunk, as the
  version specified in the GLB header only refers to the GLB container
  version.

  </div>

- `length` is the total length of the Binary glTF, including *header*
  and all *chunks*, in bytes.

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

#### 4.4.3. Chunks

<a href="#443-chunks" id="user-content-443-chunks" class="anchor"
aria-label="Permalink: 4.4.3. Chunks"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

##### 4.4.3.1. Overview

<a href="#4431-overview" id="user-content-4431-overview" class="anchor"
aria-label="Permalink: 4.4.3.1. Overview"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Each chunk has the following structure:

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div dir="auto">

<div class="highlight highlight-source-c notranslate position-relative overflow-auto"
dir="auto" snippet-clipboard-copy-content="uint32 chunkLength
uint32 chunkType
ubyte[] chunkData">

    uint32 chunkLength
    uint32 chunkType
    ubyte[] chunkData

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

- `chunkLength` is the length of `chunkData`, in bytes.

- `chunkType` indicates the type of chunk. See [Table
  1](#table-chunktypes) for details.

- `chunkData` is the binary payload of the chunk.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

The start and the end of each chunk **MUST** be aligned to a 4-byte
boundary. See chunks definitions for padding schemes. Chunks **MUST**
appear in exactly the order given in [Table 1](#table-chunktypes).

</div>

Table 1. Chunk types

|     | Chunk Type | ASCII | Description             | Occurrences |
|-----|------------|-------|-------------------------|-------------|
| 1\. | 0x4E4F534A | JSON  | Structured JSON content | 1           |
| 2\. | 0x004E4942 | BIN   | Binary buffer           | 0 or 1      |

<div dir="auto">

Client implementations **MUST** ignore chunks with unknown types to
enable glTF extensions to reference additional chunks with new types
following the first two chunks.

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

##### 4.4.3.2. Structured JSON Content

<a href="#4432-structured-json-content"
id="user-content-4432-structured-json-content" class="anchor"
aria-label="Permalink: 4.4.3.2. Structured JSON Content"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

This chunk holds the glTF JSON, as it would be provided within a .gltf
file.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 50%" />
<col style="width: 50%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><div dir="auto">
Note
</div></td>
<td><div dir="auto">
ECMAScript Implementation Note
</div>
<div dir="auto">
<p>In a JavaScript implementation, the <code>TextDecoder</code> API can
be used to extract the glTF content from the ArrayBuffer, and then the
JSON can be parsed with <code>JSON.parse</code> as usual.</p>
</div></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

This chunk **MUST** be the very first chunk of a Binary glTF asset. By
reading this chunk first, an implementation is able to progressively
retrieve resources from subsequent chunks. This way, it is also possible
to read only a selected subset of resources from a Binary glTF asset.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

This chunk **MUST** be padded with trailing `Space` chars (`0x20`) to
satisfy alignment requirements.

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

##### 4.4.3.3. Binary buffer

<a href="#4433-binary-buffer" id="user-content-4433-binary-buffer"
class="anchor" aria-label="Permalink: 4.4.3.3. Binary buffer"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

This chunk contains the binary payload for geometry, animation key
frames, skins, and images. See [GLB-stored Buffer](#glb-stored-buffer)
for details on referencing this chunk from JSON.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

This chunk **MUST** be the second chunk of the Binary glTF asset.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

This chunk **MUST** be padded with trailing zeros (`0x00`) to satisfy
alignment requirements.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

When the binary buffer is empty or when it is stored by other means,
this chunk **SHOULD** be omitted.

</div>

</div>

</div>

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

## Appendix B: BRDF Implementation

<a href="#appendix-b-brdf-implementation"
id="user-content-appendix-b-brdf-implementation" class="anchor"
aria-label="Permalink: Appendix B: BRDF Implementation"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

### B.1. General

<a href="#b1-general" id="user-content-b1-general" class="anchor"
aria-label="Permalink: B.1. General"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

This chapter presents the bidirectional reflectance distribution
function (BRDF) of the glTF 2.0 metallic-roughness material. The BRDF
describes the reflective properties of the surface of a physically based
material. For a pair of directions, the BRDF returns how much light from
the incoming direction is reflected from the surface in the outgoing
direction.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 50%" />
<col style="width: 50%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><div dir="auto">
Note
</div></td>
<td><div dir="auto">
Note
</div>
<div dir="auto">
<p>See <a href="#Pharr2016">Pharr et al. (2016), Chapter 5.6 “Surface
Reflection”</a>, for an introduction to radiometry and the BRDF.</p>
</div></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

The BRDF of the metallic-roughness material is a linear interpolation of
a metallic BRDF and a dielectric BRDF. The BRDFs share the parameters
for roughness and base color. The blending factor `metallic` describes
the metalness of the material.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div dir="auto">

<div class="highlight highlight-source-c notranslate position-relative overflow-auto"
dir="auto"
snippet-clipboard-copy-content="material = mix(dielectric_brdf, metal_brdf, metallic)
         = (1.0 - metallic) * dielectric_brdf + metallic * metal_brdf">

    material = mix(dielectric_brdf, metal_brdf, metallic)
             = (1.0 - metallic) * dielectric_brdf + metallic * metal_brdf

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 50%" />
<col style="width: 50%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><div dir="auto">
Note
</div></td>
<td><div dir="auto">
Note
</div>
<div dir="auto">
<p>Such a material model based on a linear interpolation of metallic and
dielectric components was introduced by <a href="#Burley2012">Burley
(2012)</a> and adapted by many renderers, resulting in a wide range of
applications supporting it.</p>
</div>
<div dir="auto">
<p>Usually, a material is either metallic or dielectric. A texture
provided for <code>metallic</code> with either <code>1.0</code> or
<code>0.0</code> separates metallic from dielectric regions on the mesh.
There are situations in which there is no clear separation. It may
happen that due to anti-aliasing or mip-mapping there is a portion of
metal and a portion of dielectric within a texel. Furthermore, a
material composed of several semi-transparent layers may be represented
as a blend between several single-layered materials (layering via
parameter blending).</p>
</div></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

The logical structure of the material is presented below, using an
abstract notation that describes the material as a directed acyclic
graph (DAG). The vertices correspond to the basic building blocks of the
material model: BRDFs, mixing operators, input parameters, and
constants. This is followed by an informative sample implementation as a
set of equations and source code for the BRDFs and mixing operators.

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

### B.2. Material Structure

<a href="#b2-material-structure" id="user-content-b2-material-structure"
class="anchor" aria-label="Permalink: B.2. Material Structure"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

#### B.2.1. Metals

<a href="#b21-metals" id="user-content-b21-metals" class="anchor"
aria-label="Permalink: B.2.1. Metals"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Metallic surfaces reflect most illumination, only a small portion of the
light is absorbed by the material.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 50%" />
<col style="width: 50%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><div dir="auto">
Note
</div></td>
<td><div dir="auto">
Note
</div>
<div dir="auto">
<p>See <a href="#Pharr2016">Pharr et al. (2016), Chapter 8.2 “Specular
Reflection and Transmission”</a>.</p>
</div></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

This effect is described by the Fresnel term `conductor_fresnel` with
the wavelength-dependent refractive index and extinction coefficient. To
make parameterization simple, the metallic-roughness material combines
the two quantities into a single, user-defined color value `baseColor`
that defines the reflection color at normal incidence, also referred to
as `f0`. The reflection color at grazing incidence is called `f90`. It
is set to `1.0` because the grazing angle reflectance for any material
approaches pure white in the limit. The conductor Fresnel term modulates
the contribution of a specular BRDF parameterized by the `roughness`
parameter.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div dir="auto">

<div class="highlight highlight-source-c notranslate position-relative overflow-auto"
dir="auto" snippet-clipboard-copy-content="metal_brdf =
  conductor_fresnel(
    f0 = baseColor,
    bsdf = specular_brdf(
      α = roughness ^ 2))">

    metal_brdf =
      conductor_fresnel(
        f0 = baseColor,
        bsdf = specular_brdf(
          α = roughness ^ 2))

</div>

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

#### B.2.2. Dielectrics

<a href="#b22-dielectrics" id="user-content-b22-dielectrics"
class="anchor" aria-label="Permalink: B.2.2. Dielectrics"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Unlike metals, dielectric materials transmit most of the incident
illumination into the interior of the object and the Fresnel term is
parameterized only by the refractive index.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 50%" />
<col style="width: 50%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><div dir="auto">
Note
</div></td>
<td><div dir="auto">
Note
</div>
<div dir="auto">
<p>See <a href="#Pharr2016">Pharr et al. (2016), Chapter 8.2 “Specular
Reflection and Transmission”</a>.</p>
</div></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

This makes dielectrics like glass, oil, water or air transparent. Other
dielectrics, like most plastic materials, are filled with particles that
absorb or scatter most or all of the transmitted light, reducing the
transparency and giving the surface its colorful appearance.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

As a result, dielectric materials are modeled as a Fresnel-weighted
combination of a specular BRDF, simulating the reflection at the
surface, and a diffuse BRDF, simulating the transmitted portion of the
light that is absorbed and scattered inside the object. The reflection
roughness is given by the squared `roughness` of the material. The color
of the diffuse BRDF comes from the `baseColor`. The amount of reflection
compared to transmission is directional-dependent and as such determined
by the Fresnel term. Its index of refraction is set to a fixed value of
`1.5`, a good compromise for most opaque, dielectric materials.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div dir="auto">

<div class="highlight highlight-source-c notranslate position-relative overflow-auto"
dir="auto" snippet-clipboard-copy-content="dielectric_brdf =
  fresnel_mix(
    ior = 1.5,
    base = diffuse_brdf(
      color = baseColor),
    layer = specular_brdf(
      α = roughness ^ 2))">

    dielectric_brdf =
      fresnel_mix(
        ior = 1.5,
        base = diffuse_brdf(
          color = baseColor),
        layer = specular_brdf(
          α = roughness ^ 2))

</div>

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

#### B.2.3. Microfacet Surfaces

<a href="#b23-microfacet-surfaces"
id="user-content-b23-microfacet-surfaces" class="anchor"
aria-label="Permalink: B.2.3. Microfacet Surfaces"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

The metal BRDF and the dielectric BRDF are based on a microfacet model.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 50%" />
<col style="width: 50%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><div dir="auto">
Note
</div></td>
<td><div dir="auto">
Note
</div>
<div dir="auto">
<p>The theory behind microfacet models was developed in early works by
<a href="#TorranceSparrow1967">Torrance and Sparrow (1967)</a>, <a
href="#CookTorrance1982">Cook and Torrance (1982)</a> and others.</p>
</div></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

A microfacet model describes the orientation of tiny facets
(microfacets) on the surface as a statistical distribution. The
distribution determines the orientation of the facets as a random
perturbation around the normal direction of the surface. The
perturbation strength depends on the `roughness` parameter and varies
between `0.0` (smooth surface) and `1.0` (rough surface). A number of
distribution functions have been proposed in the last decades.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

The Trowbridge-Reitz / GGX microfacet distribution describes the
microsurface as being composed of perfectly specular, infinitesimal
oblate ellipsoids, whose half-height in the normal direction is α times
the radius in the tangent plane. α = 1 gives spheres, which results in
uniform reflection in all directions. This reflection behavior
corresponds to a rough surface. α = 0 gives a perfectly specular
surface.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 50%" />
<col style="width: 50%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><div dir="auto">
Note
</div></td>
<td><div dir="auto">
Note
</div>
<div dir="auto">
<p>The Trowbridge-Reitz distribution was first described by <a
href="#TrowbridgeReitz1975">Trowbridge and Reitz (1975)</a>. Later <a
href="#Walter2007">Walter et al. (2007)</a> independently developed the
same distribution and called it “GGX”. They show that it is a better fit
for measured data than the Beckmann distribution used by <a
href="#CookTorrance1982">Cook and Torrance (1982)</a> due to its
stronger tails.</p>
</div></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

The mapping α = `roughness`<sup>2</sup> results in more perceptually
linear changes in the roughness.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 50%" />
<col style="width: 50%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><div dir="auto">
Note
</div></td>
<td><div dir="auto">
Note
</div>
<div dir="auto">
<p>This mapping was suggested by <a href="#Burley2012">Burley
(2012)</a>.</p>
</div></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

The distribution only describes the proportion of each normal on the
microsurface. It does not describe how the normals are organized. For
this we need a microsurface profile.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 50%" />
<col style="width: 50%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><div dir="auto">
Note
</div></td>
<td><div dir="auto">
Note
</div>
<div dir="auto">
<p>The difference between distribution and profile is detailed by <a
href="#Heitz2014">Heitz (2014)</a>, where he in addition provides an
extensive study of common microfacet profiles. Based on this work, we
suggest using the Smith microsurface profile (originally developed by <a
href="#Smith1967">Smith (1967)</a>) and its corresponding
masking-shadowing function. Heitz describes the Smith profile as the
most accurate model for reflection from random height fields. It assumes
that height and normal between neighboring points are not correlated,
implying a random set of microfacets instead of a continuous
surface.</p>
</div>
<div dir="auto">
<p>Microfacet models often do not consider multiple scattering. The
shadowing term suppresses light that intersects the microsurface a
second time. <a href="#Heitz2016">Heitz et al. (2016)</a> extended the
Smith-based microfacet models to include a multiple scattering
component, which significantly improves accuracy of predictions of the
model. We suggest to incorporate multiple scattering whenever possible,
either by making use of the unbiased stochastic evaluation introduced by
Heitz, or one of the approximations presented later, for example by <a
href="#KullaConty2017">Kulla and Conty (2017)</a> or <a
href="#Turquin2019">Turquin (2019)</a>.</p>
</div></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

#### B.2.4. Complete Model

<a href="#b24-complete-model" id="user-content-b24-complete-model"
class="anchor" aria-label="Permalink: B.2.4. Complete Model"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

The BRDFs and mixing operators used in the metallic-roughness material
are summarized in the following figure.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div dir="auto">

<a href="/KhronosGroup/glTF/blob/main/specification/2.0/figures/pbr.svg"
target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer"><img
src="/KhronosGroup/glTF/raw/main/specification/2.0/figures/pbr.svg"
style="max-width: 100%;" alt="pbr" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Figure 9. BRDFs and Mixing Operators

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

The glTF Specification is designed to allow applications to choose
different lighting implementations based on their requirements. Some
implementations **MAY** focus on an accurate simulation of light
transport while others **MAY** choose to deliver real-time performance.
Therefore, any implementation that adheres to the rules for mixing BRDFs
is conformant to the glTF Specification.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

In a physically accurate light simulation, the BRDFs **MUST** follow
some basic principles: the BRDF **MUST** be positive, reciprocal, and
energy conserving. This ensures that the visual output of the simulation
is independent of the underlying rendering algorithm, if it is unbiased.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

The unbiased light simulation with physically realistic BRDFs will be
the ground-truth for approximations in real-time renderers that are
often biased, but still give visually pleasing results.

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

### B.3. Sample Implementation (Informative)

<a href="#b3-sample-implementation-informative"
id="user-content-b3-sample-implementation-informative" class="anchor"
aria-label="Permalink: B.3. Sample Implementation (Informative)"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

#### B.3.1. Overview

<a href="#b31-overview" id="user-content-b31-overview" class="anchor"
aria-label="Permalink: B.3.1. Overview"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Often, renderers use approximations to solve the rendering equation,
like the split-sum approximation for image based lighting, or simplify
the math to save instructions and reduce register pressure. However,
there are many ways to achieve good approximations, depending on the
platform.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

A sample implementation is available at
<https://github.com/KhronosGroup/glTF-Sample-Viewer/> and provides an
example of a WebGL 2.0 implementation of a standard BRDF based on the
glTF material parameters. To achieve high performance in real-time
applications, this implementation uses several approximations and uses
non-physical simplifications that break energy-conservation and
reciprocity.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

We use the following notation:

</div>

<div dir="auto">

- **V** is the normalized vector from the shading location to the eye

- **L** is the normalized vector from the shading location to the light

- **N** is the surface normal in the same space as the above values

- **H** is the half vector, where **H** = normalize(**L** + **V**)

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

#### B.3.2. Specular BRDF

<a href="#b32-specular-brdf" id="user-content-b32-specular-brdf"
class="anchor" aria-label="Permalink: B.3.2. Specular BRDF"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 50%" />
<col style="width: 50%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><div dir="auto">
Note
</div></td>
<td><div dir="auto">
Note
</div>
<div dir="auto">
<p>This section contains formulas that may not display correctly in all
preview tools. View the full <a
href="https://www.khronos.org/registry/glTF/specs/2.0/glTF-2.0.html#specular-brdf"
rel="nofollow">Specular BRDF Section</a>.</p>
</div></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

The specular reflection `specular_brdf(α)` is a microfacet BRDF

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div dir="auto">

\\\text{MicrofacetBRDF} = \frac{G D}{4 \\ \left\|N \cdot L \right\| \\
\left\| N \cdot V \right\|}\\

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

with the Trowbridge-Reitz/GGX microfacet distribution

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div dir="auto">

\\D = \frac{\alpha^2 \\ \chi^{+}(N \cdot H)}{\pi ((N \cdot H)^2
(\alpha^2 - 1) + 1)^2}\\

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

and the height-correlated form of the Smith joint masking-shadowing
function

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div dir="auto">

\\G = \frac{2 \\ \left\| N \cdot L \right\| \\ \left\| N \cdot V
\right\| \\ \chi^{+}(H \cdot L) \\ \chi^{+}(H \cdot V)}{\left\| N \cdot
V \right\| \\ \sqrt{\alpha^2 + (1 - \alpha^2) (N \cdot L)^2} + \left\| N
\cdot L \right\| \\ \sqrt{\alpha^2 + (1 - \alpha^2) (N \cdot V)^2}}\\

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

where χ<sup>+</sup>(**x**) denotes the Heaviside function: 1 if **x** \>
0 and 0 if **x** ⇐ 0. See [Heitz (2014)](#Heitz2014) for a derivation of
the formulas.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Introducing the visibility function \\\nu\\

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div dir="auto">

\\\nu = \frac{G}{4 \\ \left\| N \cdot L \right\| \\ \left\| N \cdot V
\right\|}\\

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

simplifies the original microfacet BRDF to

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div dir="auto">

\\\text{MicrofacetBRDF} = \nu D\\

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

with

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div dir="auto">

\\\nu = \frac{\chi^{+}(H \cdot L) \\ \chi^{+}(H \cdot V)}{2 \\ (\left\|
N \cdot V \right\| \\ \sqrt{\alpha^2 + (1 - \alpha^2) (N \cdot L)^2} +
\left\| N \cdot L \right\| \\ \sqrt{\alpha^2 + (1 - \alpha^2) (N \cdot
V)^2})}\\

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Thus, we have the function

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div dir="auto">

<div class="highlight highlight-source-c notranslate position-relative overflow-auto"
dir="auto" snippet-clipboard-copy-content="function specular_brdf(α) {
  return Vis * D
}">

    function specular_brdf(α) {
      return Vis * D
    }

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 50%" />
<col style="width: 50%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><div dir="auto">
Note
</div></td>
<td><div dir="auto">
<p>A roughness of zero (α = 0) cannot be evaluated directly with this
formulation. As α approaches zero, the GGX distribution \(D\) collapses
to a delta function and the BRDF becomes singular, leading to divisions
by zero or numerically unstable results. Implementations should
therefore never use α = 0 in the equations above. Instead, α should be
clamped to a small positive value, or the surface should be handled as
an ideal specular (mirror) reflector using a separate code path.</p>
</div></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

#### B.3.3. Diffuse BRDF

<a href="#b33-diffuse-brdf" id="user-content-b33-diffuse-brdf"
class="anchor" aria-label="Permalink: B.3.3. Diffuse BRDF"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 50%" />
<col style="width: 50%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><div dir="auto">
Note
</div></td>
<td><div dir="auto">
Note
</div>
<div dir="auto">
<p>This section contains formulas that may not display correctly in all
preview tools. View the full <a
href="https://www.khronos.org/registry/glTF/specs/2.0/glTF-2.0.html#diffuse-brdf"
rel="nofollow">Diffuse BRDF Section</a>.</p>
</div></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

The diffuse reflection `diffuse_brdf(color)` is a Lambertian BRDF

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div dir="auto">

\\\text{LambertianBRDF} = \frac{1}{\pi}\\

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

multiplied with the `color`.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div dir="auto">

<div class="highlight highlight-source-c notranslate position-relative overflow-auto"
dir="auto"
snippet-clipboard-copy-content="function diffuse_brdf(color) {
  return (1/pi) * color
}">

    function diffuse_brdf(color) {
      return (1/pi) * color
    }

</div>

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

#### B.3.4. Fresnel

<a href="#b34-fresnel" id="user-content-b34-fresnel" class="anchor"
aria-label="Permalink: B.3.4. Fresnel"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 50%" />
<col style="width: 50%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><div dir="auto">
Note
</div></td>
<td><div dir="auto">
Note
</div>
<div dir="auto">
<p>This section contains formulas that may not display correctly in all
preview tools. View the full <a
href="https://www.khronos.org/registry/glTF/specs/2.0/glTF-2.0.html#fresnel"
rel="nofollow">Fresnel Section</a>.</p>
</div></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

An inexpensive approximation for the Fresnel term that can be used for
conductors and dielectrics was developed by [Schlick
(1994)](#Schlick1994):

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div dir="auto">

\\F = f_0 + (1 - f_0) (1 - \left\| V \cdot H \right\| )^5\\

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

The conductor Fresnel `conductor_fresnel(f0, bsdf)` applies a
view-dependent tint to a BSDF:

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div dir="auto">

<div class="highlight highlight-source-c notranslate position-relative overflow-auto"
dir="auto"
snippet-clipboard-copy-content="function conductor_fresnel(f0, bsdf) {
  return bsdf * (f0 + (1 - f0) * (1 - abs(VdotH))^5)
}">

    function conductor_fresnel(f0, bsdf) {
      return bsdf * (f0 + (1 - f0) * (1 - abs(VdotH))^5)
    }

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

For the dielectric BRDF a diffuse component `base` and a specular
component `layer` are combined via `fresnel_mix(ior, base, layer)`. The
`f0` color is now derived from the index of refraction `ior`.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div dir="auto">

<div class="highlight highlight-source-c notranslate position-relative overflow-auto"
dir="auto"
snippet-clipboard-copy-content="function fresnel_mix(ior, base, layer) {
  f0 = ((1-ior)/(1+ior))^2
  fr = f0 + (1 - f0)*(1 - abs(VdotH))^5
  return mix(base, layer, fr)
}">

    function fresnel_mix(ior, base, layer) {
      f0 = ((1-ior)/(1+ior))^2
      fr = f0 + (1 - f0)*(1 - abs(VdotH))^5
      return mix(base, layer, fr)
    }

</div>

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

#### B.3.5. Metal BRDF and Dielectric BRDF

<a href="#b35-metal-brdf-and-dielectric-brdf"
id="user-content-b35-metal-brdf-and-dielectric-brdf" class="anchor"
aria-label="Permalink: B.3.5. Metal BRDF and Dielectric BRDF"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Now that we have an implementation for all the functions used in the
glTF metallic-roughness material model, we are able to connect the
functions according to the graph shown in section [“Complete
Model”](#complete-model). By substituting the mixing functions
(`fresnel_mix`, `conductor_fresnel`) for the implementation, we arrive
at the following BRDFs for the metal and the dielectric component:

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div dir="auto">

<div class="highlight highlight-source-c notranslate position-relative overflow-auto"
dir="auto"
snippet-clipboard-copy-content="metal_brdf = specular_brdf(roughness^2) * (baseColor.rgb + (1 - baseColor.rgb) * (1 - abs(VdotH))^5)
dielectric_brdf = mix(diffuse_brdf(baseColor.rgb), specular_brdf(roughness^2), 0.04 + (1 - 0.04) * (1 - abs(VdotH))^5)">

    metal_brdf = specular_brdf(roughness^2) * (baseColor.rgb + (1 - baseColor.rgb) * (1 - abs(VdotH))^5)
    dielectric_brdf = mix(diffuse_brdf(baseColor.rgb), specular_brdf(roughness^2), 0.04 + (1 - 0.04) * (1 - abs(VdotH))^5)

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Note that the dielectric index of refraction `ior = 1.5` is now
`f0 = 0.04`.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Metal and dielectric are mixed according to the metalness:

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div dir="auto">

<div class="highlight highlight-source-c notranslate position-relative overflow-auto"
dir="auto"
snippet-clipboard-copy-content="material = mix(dielectric_brdf, metal_brdf, metallic)">

    material = mix(dielectric_brdf, metal_brdf, metallic)

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

The full code is given below:

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div dir="auto">

<div class="highlight highlight-source-c notranslate position-relative overflow-auto"
dir="auto"
snippet-clipboard-copy-content="fresnel_w = (1 - abs(VdotH))^5

diffuse_brdf = (1 / π) * baseColor.rgb
specular_brdf = D(roughness^2) * G(roughness^2) / (4 * abs(VdotN) * abs(LdotN))

dielectric_f0 = 0.04
dielectric_fresnel = dielectric_f0 + (1 - dielectric_f0) * fresnel_w
dielectric_brdf = mix(diffuse_brdf, specular_brdf, dielectric_fresnel)

metal_fresnel = baseColor.rgb + (1 - baseColor.rgb) * fresnel_w
metal_brdf = metal_fresnel * specular_brdf

material = mix(dielectric_brdf, metal_brdf, metallic)">

    fresnel_w = (1 - abs(VdotH))^5

    diffuse_brdf = (1 / π) * baseColor.rgb
    specular_brdf = D(roughness^2) * G(roughness^2) / (4 * abs(VdotN) * abs(LdotN))

    dielectric_f0 = 0.04
    dielectric_fresnel = dielectric_f0 + (1 - dielectric_f0) * fresnel_w
    dielectric_brdf = mix(diffuse_brdf, specular_brdf, dielectric_fresnel)

    metal_fresnel = baseColor.rgb + (1 - baseColor.rgb) * fresnel_w
    metal_brdf = metal_fresnel * specular_brdf

    material = mix(dielectric_brdf, metal_brdf, metallic)

</div>

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

#### B.3.6. Discussion

<a href="#b36-discussion" id="user-content-b36-discussion"
class="anchor" aria-label="Permalink: B.3.6. Discussion"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

##### B.3.6.1. Masking-Shadowing Term and Multiple Scattering

<a href="#b361-masking-shadowing-term-and-multiple-scattering"
id="user-content-b361-masking-shadowing-term-and-multiple-scattering"
class="anchor"
aria-label="Permalink: B.3.6.1. Masking-Shadowing Term and Multiple Scattering"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

The model for specular reflection can be improved in several ways.
[Heitz (2014)](#Heitz2014) notes that a more accurate form of the
masking-shadowing function takes the correlation between masking and
shadowing due to the height of the microsurface into account. This
correlation is accounted for in the height-correlated masking and
shadowing function. Another improvement in accuracy can be achieved by
modeling multiple scattering, see Section [Microfacet
Surfaces](#microfacet-surfaces).

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

##### B.3.6.2. Schlick’s Fresnel Approximation

<a href="#b362-schlicks-fresnel-approximation"
id="user-content-b362-schlicks-fresnel-approximation" class="anchor"
aria-label="Permalink: B.3.6.2. Schlick’s Fresnel Approximation"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Although Schlick’s Fresnel is a good approximation for a wide range of
metallic and dielectric materials, there are a couple of reasons to use
a more sophisticated solution for the Fresnel term.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Metals often exhibit a “dip” in reflectance near grazing angles, which
is not present in the Schlick Fresnel. [Lazányi and Szirmay-Kalos
(2005)](#LazanyiSzirmayKalos2005) extend the Schlick Fresnel with an
error term to account for it. [Hoffman (2019)](#Hoffman2019) improves
the parameterization of this term by introducing an artist-friendly
`f82` color, the color at an angle of about 82°. An additional color
parameter for metals was also introduced by [Gulbrandsen
(2014)](#Gulbrandsen2014). Gulbrandson calls it “edge tint” and uses it
in the full Fresnel equations instead of Schlick’s approximation. Even
though the full Fresnel equations should give a more accurate result,
Hoffman shows that it is worse than Schlick’s approximation in the
context of RGB renderers. As we target RGB renderers and do not provide
an additional color parameter for metals in glTF, we suggest using the
original Schlick Fresnel for metals.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

The index of refraction of most dielectrics is 1.5. For that reason, the
dielectric Fresnel term uses a fixed `f0 = 0.04`. The Schlick Fresnel
approximates the full Fresnel equations well for an index of refraction
in the range \[1.2, 2.2\]. The main reason for a material to fall
outside this range is transparency and nested objects. If a transparent
object overlaps another transparent object and both have the same (or
similar) index of refraction, the resulting ratio at the boundary is 1
(or close to 1). According to the full Fresnel equations, there is no
(or almost no) reflection in this case. The reflection intensity
computed from the Schlick Fresnel approximation will be too high.
Implementations that care about accuracy in case of nested dielectrics
are encouraged to use the full Fresnel equations for dielectrics. For
metals Schlick’s approximation is still a good choice.

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

##### B.3.6.3. Coupling Diffuse and Specular Reflection

<a href="#b363-coupling-diffuse-and-specular-reflection"
id="user-content-b363-coupling-diffuse-and-specular-reflection"
class="anchor"
aria-label="Permalink: B.3.6.3. Coupling Diffuse and Specular Reflection"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

While the coupling of diffuse and specular components in `fresnel_mix`
as proposed in this section is simple and cheap to compute, it is not
very accurate and breaks a fundamental property that a physically based
BRDF must fulfill — energy conservation. Energy conservation means that
a BRDF must not reflect more light than it receives. Several fixes have
been proposed, each with its own trade-offs regarding performance and
quality.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

[Burley (2012)](#Burley2012) notes that a common solution found in many
models calculates the diffuse Fresnel factor by evaluating the Fresnel
term twice with view and light direction instead of the half vector:
`(1-F(NdotL)) * (1-F(NdotV))`. While this is energy-conserving, he notes
that this weighting results in significant darkening at grazing angles,
an effect they couldn’t observe in their measurements. They propose some
changes to the diffuse BRDF to make it better predict the measurements,
but even the fixed version is still not energy conserving
mathematically.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

More recently, [Jakob et al. (2014)](#Jakob2014) developed a generic
framework for computing BSDFs of layered materials, including multiple
scattering within layers. Amongst much more complicated scenarios it
also solves the special case of coupling diffuse and specular
components, but it is too heavy for textured materials, even in offline
rendering.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

[Kulla and Conty (2017)](#KullaConty2017) found a solution tailored to
the special case of coupling diffuse and specular components, which is
easy to compute. It requires the directional albedo of the
Fresnel-weighted specular BRDF to be precomputed and tabulated, but they
found that the function is smooth, and a low-resolution 3D texture (16³
pixels) is sufficient. Their coupled diffuse-specular model is not only
energy-*con*serving, but also energy-*pre*serving, meaning that if
neither the specular nor the diffuse component absorb any energy, all
energy is reflected.

</div>

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

## Appendix C: Animation Sampler Interpolation Modes

<a href="#appendix-c-animation-sampler-interpolation-modes"
id="user-content-appendix-c-animation-sampler-interpolation-modes"
class="anchor"
aria-label="Permalink: Appendix C: Animation Sampler Interpolation Modes"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

### C.1. Overview

<a href="#c1-overview" id="user-content-c1-overview" class="anchor"
aria-label="Permalink: C.1. Overview"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 50%" />
<col style="width: 50%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><div dir="auto">
Note
</div></td>
<td><div dir="auto">
Note
</div>
<div dir="auto">
<p>This appendix contains formulas that may not display correctly in all
preview tools. View the full <a
href="https://www.khronos.org/registry/glTF/specs/2.0/glTF-2.0.html#appendix-c-interpolation"
rel="nofollow">Appendix C: Animation Sampler Interpolation
Modes</a>.</p>
</div></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Animation sampler interpolation modes define how to compute values of
animated properties for the timestamps located between the keyframes.
When the current (requested) timestamp exists in the animation data, its
associated property value **MUST** be used as-is, without interpolation.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

For the following sections, let

</div>

<div dir="auto">

- \\n\\ be the total number of keyframes, \\n \> 0\\;

- \\t_k\\ be the timestamp of the \\k\\-th keyframe, \\k \in \[1,n\]\\;

- \\v_k\\ be the animated property value of the \\k\\-th keyframe;

- \\t_c\\ be the current (requested) timestamp, \\t_k \< t_c \<
  t\_{k+1}\\;

- \\t_d = t\_{k + 1} - t_k\\ be the duration of the interpolation
  segment;

- \\t = (t_c - t_k) / t_d\\ be the segment-normalized interpolation
  factor.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

The scalar-vector multiplications are per vector component.

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

### C.2. Step Interpolation

<a href="#c2-step-interpolation" id="user-content-c2-step-interpolation"
class="anchor" aria-label="Permalink: C.2. Step Interpolation"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

This mode is used when the animation sampler interpolation mode is set
to `STEP`.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

The interpolated sampler value \\v_t\\ at the current (requested)
timestamp \\t_c\\ is computed as follows.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div dir="auto">

\\v_t = v_k\\

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

### C.3. Linear Interpolation

<a href="#c3-linear-interpolation"
id="user-content-c3-linear-interpolation" class="anchor"
aria-label="Permalink: C.3. Linear Interpolation"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

This mode is used when the animation sampler interpolation mode is set
to `LINEAR` and the animated property is not `rotation`.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

The interpolated sampler value \\v_t\\ at the current (requested)
timestamp \\t_c\\ is computed as follows.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div dir="auto">

\\v_t = (1 - t) \* v_k + t \* v\_{k+1}\\

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

### C.4. Spherical Linear Interpolation

<a href="#c4-spherical-linear-interpolation"
id="user-content-c4-spherical-linear-interpolation" class="anchor"
aria-label="Permalink: C.4. Spherical Linear Interpolation"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

This mode is used when the animation sampler interpolation mode is set
to `LINEAR` and the animated property is `rotation`, i.e., values of the
animated property are unit quaternions.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Let

</div>

<div dir="auto">

- \\a = arccos(\|v_k \cdot v\_{k+1}\|)\\ be the arccosine of the
  absolute value of the dot product of two consecutive quaternions;

- \\s = \frac{v_k \cdot v\_{k+1}}{\|v_k \cdot v\_{k+1}\|}\\ be the sign
  of the dot product of two consecutive quaternions.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

The interpolated sampler value \\v_t\\ at the timestamp \\t_c\\ is
computed as follows.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div dir="auto">

\\v_t = \frac{sin(a(1 - t))}{sin(a)} \* v_k + s \*
\frac{sin(at)}{sin(a)} \* v\_{k+1}\\

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 50%" />
<col style="width: 50%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><div dir="auto">
Note
</div></td>
<td><div dir="auto">
Implementation Note
</div>
<div dir="auto">
<p>Using the dot product’s absolute value for computing \$a\$ and
multiplying \$v_{k+1}\$ by the dot product’s sign ensure that the
spherical interpolation follows the short path along the great circle
defined by the two quaternions.</p>
</div></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Implementations **MAY** approximate these equations to reach
application-specific accuracy and/or performance targets.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 50%" />
<col style="width: 50%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><div dir="auto">
Note
</div></td>
<td><div dir="auto">
Implementation Note
</div>
<div dir="auto">
<p>When \$a\$ is close to zero, spherical linear interpolation turns
into regular linear interpolation.</p>
</div></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto">

### C.5. Cubic Spline Interpolation

<a href="#c5-cubic-spline-interpolation"
id="user-content-c5-cubic-spline-interpolation" class="anchor"
aria-label="Permalink: C.5. Cubic Spline Interpolation"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
class="octicon octicon-link" /></a>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

This mode is used when the animation sampler interpolation mode is set
to `CUBICSPLINE`.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

An animation sampler that uses cubic spline interpolation **MUST** have
at least 2 keyframes.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

For each timestamp stored in the animation sampler, there are three
associated keyframe values: in-tangent, property value, and out-tangent.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

Let

</div>

<div dir="auto">

- \\a_k\\, \\v_k\\, and \\b_k\\ be the in-tangent, the property value,
  and the out-tangent of the \\k\\-th frame respectively.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

The interpolated sampler value \\v_t\\ at the timestamp \\t_c\\ is
computed as follows.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<div dir="auto">

\\v_t = (2t^3 - 3t^2 + 1) \* v_k + t_d(t^3 - 2t^2 + t) \* b_k + (-2t^3 +
3t^2) \* v\_{k+1} + t_d(t^3 - t^2) \* a\_{k+1}\\

</div>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

When the animation sampler targets a node’s rotation property, the
interpolated quaternion **MUST** be normalized before applying the
result to the node’s rotation.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

When writing out rotation values, exporters **SHOULD** take care to not
write out values that can result in an invalid quaternion with all zero
values being produced by the interpolation.

</div>

<div dir="auto">

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 50%" />
<col style="width: 50%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><div dir="auto">
Note
</div></td>
<td><div dir="auto">
Implementation Note
</div>
<div dir="auto">
<p>This can be achieved by ensuring that \$v_k != -v_{k+1}\$ for all
keyframes.</p>
</div></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

</div>

<div dir="auto">

The first in-tangent \\a_1\\ and last out-tangent \\b_n\\ **SHOULD** be
zeros as they are not used in the spline calculations.

</div>

</div>

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div class="d-none">

</div>

</div>

</div>

</div>

</div>

</div>

</div>

</div>

</div>

</div>

</div>
